The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office announced more than 50 arrests following a multi-agency, multi-day operation targeting human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county. Operation Late Checkout ran from Sept. 13 in Indian River County. The operation netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers, Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a press conference on Thursday. Flowers announced the results alongside a representative from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. “Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office, Seminole County Sheriff’s Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney’s Office,” Flowers said. The operation’s targeted goal was stopping human trafficking in the Indian River County area, the sheriff’s office said. During the operation, several victims were identified, and investigators said ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time. One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online. “Our team did a great job of getting him off the street,” Flowers said. Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation, the sheriff’s office said. Victims’ advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were also on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked. “We have many ongoing investigations as a result of this,” Flowers said. Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County. “We’ve never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot,” he said. FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county. “This operation shows that within our communities there are dangerous individuals committing heinous crimes who think they can get away with it,” Williams said. Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors. “Our work is far from done,” Williams said. “This operation requires a lot of resources and time. We cannot do this work alone, and our success depends on the great partnership and collaboration that you see today.” FDLE said it houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks, Frank Frangella still carries the memories of what he witnessed at Ground Zero. The Martin County School District's Director of Safety & Security was a New York City Police Department officer when terrorists struck the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001.WATCH BELOW:"It's always there and there are always little things that remind you of what happened," Frangella said from his office, surrounded by photos, statues and a book of memories honoring those lost in the attacks.Frangella was asleep after working the midnight shift when his wife woke him with news that would change his life forever."I was actually asleep when the first plane hit and my wife woke me up and she goes – a plane just hit the World Trade Center," Frangella recalled. "There was a big hole in that building and I knew right away what that was, so I just started dressing."The weather that morning remains etched in his memory. "The one thing I remember from that day, soon as I walked out of the house – it was the most beautiful day in the world. There wasn't a cloud in the sky, and I'm thinking to myself driving to where I was going – how can this happen on such a beautiful day."Initially assigned to help intake victims at a Staten Island triage area, Frangella waited for hours as no injured survivors arrived. "It was like what's happening, you know. We're not getting any information."With communication systems failing, Frangella and fellow officers decided to take a boat directly to Ground Zero. What they found defied comprehension."By that time, both buildings were down. And I mean - it looked like a war zone," he said. "It was literally a pile, and it was huge."The scale of destruction was unlike anything Frangella had ever seen. "You figure two of the largest buildings in Manhattan, you didn't see a desk. Nothing that resembled an office building," he said. "Everything was pulverized."SPECIAL COVERAGE: Remembering 9/11What began as a rescue mission quickly became a recovery operation, according to Frangella. "Everybody that was down there was doing it because they wanted to save lives, and then we found out pretty quickly on that there was no lives to save, and it was a recovery mission more than anything else."Despite their efforts, Frangella's team did not find any survivors.The emotional toll of those days followed Frangella home to his family. "A few weeks later, I remember sitting home and it all hit. I just started crying and I don't even know why I was crying," he said.The dust-covered uniforms from Ground Zero created an unexpected memorial in the Frangella household. "We had a washing machine in the basement that she was washing all my clothing with and how many souls were in that wash. So, it was almost like a shrine in my house. We never used it again after 9/11 because it was like – it just felt wrong to use it."Today, Frangella applies his experience from that tragic day to his role protecting Martin County's school children. He often shares his story with students, creating powerful moments of connection."This little girl about this big walks over to me and she says -- can I hug you? When that little girl came over, there wasn't a dry eye in the house. I mean everybody started crying and she just said… thank you. It was the most amazing thing in the world," Frangella said.Despite his role in the response efforts, Frangella has never visited the 9/11 Memorial and Museum. "I was there when it happened. I don't need to relive it again," he said.As the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks approaches, first responders like Frangella continue processing their experiences while serving their communities in new ways. His transition from protecting New York City to safeguarding Martin County schools demonstrates how the impact of that day continues to shape public service careers across the country.Twenty-five years later, Frangella honors not just his own experience, but that of every person who responded that day. "There are thousands upon thousands of stories. This is just mine," he said. "Everybody says that time heals all, and I know for me and everybody who was down there -- we're still waiting."To hear more stories be sure to watch Echoes of September: A 9/11 Special on Friday, Sept. on WPTVThis story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Martin County High School received another threat through the state's FortifyFL reporting system, the third bomb threat involving our campus this week, the school district said Friday afternoon. "I recognize that you have heard from me repeatedly this week regarding safety-related disruptions on our campus," Principal Lori Vogel said in a message to families. The latest threat referenced two specific buildings, requiring students and staff to be evacuated while law enforcement conducted a thorough search. Students and staff were relocated to other areas of campus during the response. On Monday, students and staff were evacuated after a bomb threat prompted a response from the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Eight days ago, students and staff were evacuated in the afternoon after a bomb threat was received via email, according to school officials. In a message sent to families, school officials said all buildings were being evacuated at the direction of law enforcement while authorities investigate the threat. Vogel noted the seriousness of the threats. "Every threat must be taken seriously," the principal said. "Each report generates a significant law enforcement response, disrupts instruction, displaces students and staff, and creates understandable concern throughout our school community. Unlike many situations that may require an emergency response, the behavior prompting these repeated disruptions is entirely avoidable. We need our families as partners in addressing this behavior. Please speak directly with your children about the seriousness and far-reaching impact of making or participating in a false threat." The message added: "What a student may view as a joke or a temporary way to avoid class can have widespread consequences for an entire campus and community. FortifyFL is an important safety resource. Students and families who become aware of a credible threat—or who have a legitimate reason to believe questionable, dangerous or criminal activity may be occurring—should continue to report that information through FortifyFL. Information about submitting a report is available on our school's and the School District's websites. "However, FortifyFL must never be used to submit information that someone knows to be false," the message said. "The District has zero tolerance for anyone who knowingly misuses the platform or participates in making a false threat. Any individual found responsible will face severe school disciplinary consequences and potential criminal charges." The principal concluded: "We appreciate your partnership in reinforcing that false threats are neither harmless nor funny. They place an unacceptable burden on students, employees, families, law enforcement and the broader community—and they must stop. Thank you for your immediate attention to this serious matter and for partnering with us to maintain a safe, orderly learning environment for every student and staff member at Martin County High School." Lucie County staff found at least 14 license plate reader cameras installed on county rights-of-way without a permit, and the county says it does not know who owns them. Staff shared the finding with commissioners Tuesday night in an update on the board's Sept. 1 decision to remove automated license plate readers from county-controlled property. The number of unpermitted cameras has climbed quickly. A county agenda report signed Sept. 10 said field checks had turned up three cameras at unpermitted locations. By Tuesday, staff said the count had reached at least 14, and the search is not finished. County commissioner James Clasby says the issue isn't as much about the cameras as who's receiving the data. Not knowing who they belong to, I think, is another issue. Perhaps that goes about the entirety of Flock camera reform, Clasby said. "There's the potential for non-law enforcement to have cameras out there, and I'm not okay with that. Because the county has no permit on file for those cameras, staff said it cannot identify an applicant to contact. Instead, the county is posting removal notices directly on the devices. "It's like a bright red notice that says you have 30 days to remove this. And we will also bag the cameras so they're not operable," said interim county administrator Mayte Santamaria. Staff said the county has not yet gone through its entire right-of-way and more unauthorized cameras may still be found. Staff is also double-checking some traffic signals that interact with state right-of-way, which could add a handful more. The agenda report says staff is comparing crowdsourced data from various sources against known locations to find unknown or unauthorized installations. See also: Florida boaters rescued after capsized vessel leaves them stranded in tree The unpermitted cameras are in addition to 52 devices the county previously authorized within its rights-of-way. Staff said all 52 had received revocation notices as of Monday, giving their owners 30 days to remove them. According to the report, county permit records indicate most of the authorized devices were installed on behalf of law enforcement agencies. The county shared its inventory with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, the Fort Pierce Police Department and the Port St. Lucie Police Department ahead of the notices. The report says that step was meant both to give the agencies advance notice and to let them review the data for accuracy. Staff also told commissioners there are no active applications for new devices under review. Commissioners voted 3-2 on Sept. 1 to stop issuing permits for Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers on county-owned or county-controlled property. The vote went beyond a state order that applies only to state highways. Commissioner James Clasby made the motion, which he said was about protecting residents' privacy. Commissioners Clasby, Lee and Lowry voted yes, and Chair Jamie Fowler and Commissioner Cathy Townsend voted no. The board's direction does not apply to license plate readers mounted in law enforcement vehicles or cameras on private property.

Lucie County staff are providing updates to commissioners tonight on the removal of automated license plate readers, including Flock cameras, from county-maintained roads after a vote earlier this month. Erick Gill, communications director for St. Lucie County, said letters were sent earlier this week to all permit holders, notifying them of the decision and giving them 30 days to remove the cameras. "Earlier this week, letters went out to all the permit holders, whether some of those were permits were submitted on the behalf of law enforcement agencies, some were directly manufacturers of those cameras. So, they were notified this week and have 30 days to remove those cameras from the St. Lucie County right-of-ways," Gill said. County right-of-ways include the shoulders of highways and roads maintained by the county. Gill said there were about 50 to 55 permits issued for the cameras. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis has signed a death warrant for 77-year-old William Reaves Jr., the man convicted of murdering Indian River County Sheriff’s Deputy Richard Raczkoski in 1986. The execution is scheduled for Tuesday, Oct. Reaves was convicted of murdereing Raczkoski on Sept. 23, 1986, after a confrontation at a convenience store. Deputy Raczkoski had responded to a 911 call at the store when he encountered Reaves. During a conversation between the two, a gun fell from Reaves’s shorts. Deputy Raczkoski placed his knee on the weapon. Reaves then pushed the deputy away, grabbed the gun and pointed it at Deputy Raczkoski’s face. As Deputy Raczkoski attempted to draw his own weapon, Reaves said, “I wouldn’t do that if I were you.” The deputy backed away, turned, and ran. Reaves fired seven rounds, striking Deputy Raczkoski four times. Reaves was tried in the 19th Judicial Circuit in Indian River County. On direct appeal, the Florida Supreme Court reversed the initial conviction and remanded the case for a new trial. On remand, Reaves was again convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death on March 6, 1992, in Vero Beach. The Florida Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and death sentence on April 7, 1994. The United States Supreme Court denied Reaves’s petition for a writ of certiorari on Nov. Reaves pursued numerous postconviction challenges in both state and federal courts over the following decades. District Court for the Southern District of Florida granted Reaves’s federal petition for a writ of habeas corpus. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit overturned that ruling and ordered that the petition be denied. Additional postconviction motions and petitions were subsequently denied, and those denials were affirmed on appeal. Executive clemency was also considered and denied. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, in his letter recommending the warrant, wrote that “the record is legally sufficient to support the issuance of a death warrant,” and confirmed that “there are no stays of execution issued by any court of competent jurisdiction in this cause.” The execution is scheduled to take place at Florida State Prison in Raiford. If carried out as scheduled, it will come 40 years after the murder of Deputy Raczkoski.

Lucie fulfillment center is closing Thursday for a major renovation, leaving hundreds of workers out of a job while others have transferred to different facilities. When Amazon filed its layoff notice in July, 494 employees were listed as affected. Since then, more than 200 workers have transferred to other Amazon locations, according to information provided to CBS12 News. Around 300 employees are expected to take severance as the Port St. Lucie facility shuts down. Local workforce organizations, including CareerSource Research Coast and the Economic Development Council of St. Lucie County, have spent recent months holding job fairs and helping affected workers connect with other employers. Lucie County Commissioner Cathy Townsend said the closure highlights the importance of attracting a wider range of businesses to the county. I think we need to be more strategic on the companies we want coming here, Townsend said. My focus would be more on small businesses. See also: CBS12 I-Team: Amendment 3 backers say tax relief could help Florida homeowners stay put The closure is expected to last until at least 2028. Amazon plans to invest about $200 million to renovate and expand the facility. Lucie EDC said the work will include advanced robotics and artificial intelligence capabilities, along with an additional 870,000 square feet. Amazon plans to reopen the facility in the second half of 2028 and hire more than 1,000 employees. Workers who were employed at the facility before the closure will be eligible for rehire when it reopens, according to the EDC. Amazon has said the closure is not expected to impact customers because operations will be handled by other facilities during the renovation.

A man has been sentenced to 10 years behind bars for his role in a 2024 Vero Beach shooting. According to the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office , Vandrell Jacobs, 25, was arrested on Jan. 29, 2024 following an investigation into an Indian River County shooting that took place the day prior. IRCSO says that deputies responded to reports of gunfire at the Orangewood Apartments in Vero Beach on Jan. Investigators said five bullets struck an apartment occupied by a family, and witnesses reported seeing people inside a red Mercedes firing shots towards an intended victim before fleeing. Surveillance footage shows the Mercedes stopping in the area of the shooting before driving away, and IRCSO says that Flock cameras recorded the car for about two minutes before the shooting. See also: Sebastian Police identify man killed in officer-involved shooting; FDLE investigating A deputy who responded to the shooting pursued the Mercedes, but the car fled at a high speed and ran red lights. The following day, the Mercedes was located and Jacobs was arrested. At the time, he admitted to the allegations, and was charged with shooting into a dwelling/vehicle/building and fleeing police with disregard for safety. Now, he begins a decade-long prison sentence.

A health alert, no-swim advisory and no-irrigation advisory has been issued for waterways near the Boca Raton Resort following a wastewater spill into Camino Real, connected to the Intracoastal Waterway just northwest of the resort, the Florida Department of Health in Palm Beach County announced Friday afternoon.The department said drinking water is not affected.The city of Boca Raton is coordinating testing and cleanup actions with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection, health officials said. Until further information is known regarding possible bacterial contamination, residents and visitors in the area are urged to take precautions when in contact with the affected waterways, the department said.Health officials are urging anyone who comes into contact with the water in the area to wash thoroughly, especially before eating or drinking, as water contaminated with high levels of fecal bacteria can cause disease, infections or rashes.Sensitive individuals, including children, the elderly and those who are immunocompromised, may still be at risk even at low concentrations and should avoid any exposure.For more information about the potential health effects of wastewater overflow, contact the Florida Department of Health in Palm Beach County at 561-837-5900 or CHD50ContactUs@FLHealth.gov. For after-hours questions or inquiries, call 561-881-1888.

Flooded streets, yards and canals across The Acreage and nearby communities have residents worried that more rain forecast this weekend could worsen already dangerous conditions.After roughly 9 inches of rain fell in parts of western Palm Beach County, drainage systems were overwhelmed, sending water into roads, swales and residential properties.WATCH BELOW: Residents fear more flooding after 9 inches of rain"It's a mess. It's a mess," resident Debby Duprey said as water from a nearby canal pushed toward her home. "The canal is coming right into our yard."Her husband, Rick Duprey, said the family fears the water could eventually enter the house."It's going to start to seep under and into the house," he said.Less than 12 hours later, the Dupreys were preparing for another round of rain, worried the water would rise again."I feel like it's going to creep right back up," Debby Duprey said. "I'm afraid it's going to come up through the foundation."As residents dealt with flooding, crews with the Indian Trail Improvement District worked around the clock to manage water levels, monitor canals and respond to reports of breaches and drainage problems.Elizabeth Accomando with the district said crews prepared the system before the storm and lowered canal levels where possible."Our canals were very low in most cases," Accomando said. But she said the sheer volume and intensity of the rainfall overwhelmed the system."If you think about how water works and how water drains, first of all, no matter how much you pump, if it's coming down just as fast or as much in volume, we can't pump out that fast," she said.Accomando said the district operates at the "head" of a larger interconnected drainage network that includes Royal Palm Beach, Loxahatchee Groves, Palm Beach County and the South Florida Water Management District."As we're discharging the water, which we have been, it has to flow downhill," she said. "So we have to wait for everybody at the bottom end to get drained out before we can drain." The South Florida Water Management District said its regional flood control system is operating normally and has capacity for expected weekend rainfall.In a statement, the agency said the regional system includes more than 2,300 miles of canals and 2,200 miles of berms and levees that move water from local drainage districts and municipalities.The district said it is aware of complaints involving flooding along the M Canal, which it said is not operated or maintained by South Florida Water Management. Water from that canal flows into the district-operated C-51 Canal, which officials said is currently moving stormwater from western Palm Beach County."The District's regional flood control system throughout its 16-county area of responsibility is ready for any rainfall expected this weekend and no problems have been reported with the District's flood control infrastructure," the statement said.Accomando said crews have been in the field continuously, although lightning has temporarily slowed operations."Every single person is out working, but when it's lightning, they have got to go into their trucks," she said. "They can't be out moving water in the middle of a lightning storm."The district said it has also been inundated with calls from residents seeking answers and assistance. "We have 50,000 residents, and if everybody's calling at once, it's impossible," Accomando said. "But we are paying attention."The district brought in additional staff to answer calls, emails and voicemails while field crews continued working flooded areas.Officials said the recent drought also contributed to the flooding. Accomando described current conditions as part of a "75-year drought," which left the ground compacted and less able to absorb sudden heavy rainfall."When the rain does come, it's going to be a deluge," she said. "So this is like the new normal."Some residents questioned why canals were not lowered further before the storm, but Accomando said aggressively draining canals during drought conditions can create additional problems, including unstable canal banks."Swales and canals are technically designed to hold the water until we can get it out of the district," she said. "Now we've gotten so much rain so fast that there's nothing that can hold that much water at once."Officials are urging residents not to drive through standing water and to help by clearing swales, culverts and drains near their homes."With more than 400 miles of roads and thousands of miles of canals and swales to monitor, we need residents to be our eyes," Accomando said.Despite residents' frustration and fears, district leaders said crews will continue working through the weekend as more rain remains possible.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Florida's property-tax fight is putting Gov. Ron DeSantis and law enforcement leaders on opposite sides, with supporters promising relief for homeowners and opponents warning that local services could pay the price.With a little more than six weeks until Election Day, a St. Pete Polls survey shows about 45% support for Amendment 3, roughly 30% opposition and nearly a quarter of voters undecided. Florida constitutional amendments require at least 60% approval to pass.WATCH HERE: DeSantis, sheriffs clash over Amendment 3 as poll shows support below passage thresholdThe proposal has the Florida Republican Party’s endorsement, while Florida Realtors has committed $10 million to the campaign supporting it.DeSantis, this week, acknowledged the amendment falls short of the property-tax changes he wanted. Still, he is urging voters to approve it.“But if you don't get this one passed, they're not going to give you any relief on property tax,” DeSantis said.Amendment 3 would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, reducing the portion of an eligible home’s assessed value subject to those taxes. It would also lower the annual assessment-growth cap for non-homestead properties, including rentals and commercial buildings, from 10% to 5%. Check out the Florida House analysis.Supporters argue the changes would help homeowners manage costs and that local governments can reduce spending without sacrificing essential services.But the Florida Sheriffs Association is challenging that argument with an advertising campaign warning of consequences for public safety.“We want a tax cut too, but Amendment 3 is the wrong way to do it,” the ad says.Police and firefighter groups have also joined the opposition, questioning how communities would replace the revenue supporting emergency services.“We are asking Floridians to look carefully at voting for something that sounds so appealing, but provides no clear path to fund core public safety services,” said Jennifer Cook Pritt of the Florida Police Chiefs Association, at a press event this week.A legislative analysis estimates the amendment would reduce local non-school property-tax revenue by approximately $4.95 billion in the 2027-28 fiscal year and $8.78 billion in 2028-29. Those estimates describe revenue reductions; decisions about spending and services would follow locally. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis has signed a death warrant for 77-year-old William Reaves Jr., the man convicted of murdering Indian River County Sheriff's Deputy Richard Raczkoski in 1986. The execution is scheduled for Tuesday, Oct. 20, at 6 p.m.WATCH BELOW: Man who killed Indian River Co. deputy to be executed in OctoberReaves was convicted of murdereing Raczkoski on Sept. 23, 1986, after a confrontation at a convenience store.Deputy Raczkoski had responded to a 911 call at the store when he encountered Reaves. During a conversation between the two, a gun fell from Reaves's shorts. Deputy Raczkoski placed his knee on the weapon. Reaves then pushed the deputy away, grabbed the gun and pointed it at Deputy Raczkoski's face.As Deputy Raczkoski attempted to draw his own weapon, Reaves said, "I wouldn't do that if I were you." The deputy backed away, turned, and ran. Reaves fired seven rounds, striking Deputy Raczkoski four times.Reaves was tried in the 19th Judicial Circuit in Indian River County. On direct appeal, the Florida Supreme Court reversed the initial conviction and remanded the case for a new trial. On remand, Reaves was again convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death on March 6, 1992, in Vero Beach.The Florida Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and death sentence on April 7, 1994. The United States Supreme Court denied Reaves's petition for a writ of certiorari on Nov. 7, 1994.Reaves pursued numerous postconviction challenges in both state and federal courts over the following decades.In 2015, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida granted Reaves's federal petition for a writ of habeas corpus. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit overturned that ruling and ordered that the petition be denied.Additional postconviction motions and petitions were subsequently denied, and those denials were affirmed on appeal. Executive clemency was also considered and denied.Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, in his letter recommending the warrant, wrote that "the record is legally sufficient to support the issuance of a death warrant," and confirmed that "there are no stays of execution issued by any court of competent jurisdiction in this cause."The execution is scheduled to take place at Florida State Prison in Raiford. If carried out as scheduled, it will come 40 years after the murder of Deputy Raczkoski.

Ron DeSantis signed his 18th death warrant of the year Friday. William Reaves , convicted of the 1986 killing of an Indian River County Sheriff's deputy, is set to be executed by lethal injection at Florida State Prison in Stark on Oct. According to court records, Reaves shot Deputy Sheriff Richard Raczkowski four times in the back outside a Zippy Mart convenience store near Vero Beach on September 23, 1986. Reaves had called 911 from a pay phone because he didn’t have money for a cab. Raczkowski, who was dispatched to the call, called the 911 dispatcher to order a cab for Reaves and to inquire about outstanding warrants. During this time, Reaves said a gun fell out of his pants. After the deputy attempted to block Reaves from retrieving the gun, a struggle ensued and Reaves wrestled the weapon away from Raczkowski. The deputy asked Reaves not to kill him and turned to run away, at which time Reaves fired four times into Raczkowski’s back. He would die a short time later. Reaves went to the home of a friend, who later told police Reaves confessed to shooting the deputy as he was high on cocaine and panicked. Reaves was arrested three days later at a bus stop and charged with first-degree murder, possession of a firearm by a convicted felon and trafficking in cocaine. He entered a not guilty plea but was found guilty of first-degree murder in September 1987, with the jury giving a unanimous recommendation for the death penalty. The Florida Supreme Court reversed the conviction and sentence in 1991, finding the trial court erred by allowing a prosecutor on the case who had previously defended Reaves in a criminal matter. A second jury again found Reaves guilty of first-degree murder in February 1992, with the jury voting 10-2 to recommend a death sentence. Florida leads the nation in executions, carrying out 15 of them this year after 19 were performed last year, the most in a single year by the state since the U.S. Supreme Court ended a four-year nationwide moratorium on capital punishment in 1976. Curtis Wilkie Beasley, 77, is scheduled for execution on Sept. 29 for the 1995 murder of a Polk County woman who was bludgeoned with a hammer in her home. Last Friday, DeSantis signed a warrant for William Lee Thompson, 74, to be executed Oct. 13 for the murder, kidnapping, and sexual battery of Sally Ivester more than 50 years ago in North Miami Beach. Counsel for Reaves quickly filed a motion Friday for a stay until pending motions for a stay they have also filed regarding Thompson are resolved. See also: Driver hits 120 mph on I-95 before crashing into tree, fence while fleeing FHP Both clients are due the best representation counsel can provide, particularly when both clients are facing a scheduled execution date, stated the motion from Reaves’ counsel Brittney Lacy. The state has conducted 43 executions under DeSantis, or 31 percent of the 140 carried out since 1976. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers has been pushing for DeSantis to sign the warrant for Reaves as he is one that, in my opinion, should be a priority case. "It's very frustrating as the Sheriff, Flowers told WPEC last July. We want people to know that we're holding people accountable. And in this case, yes, he's jailed, yes, he's sitting there, but ultimately it was decided a long time ago that he would face the death penalty, and it's time for him to actually face the consequences. He's exhausted all of his appeals. Many other cases just like his have resulted in execution, and for some reason, he continues to cost us taxpayer dollars every single day.

Lucie County staff found at least 14 license plate reader cameras installed on county rights-of-way without a permit, and the county says it does not know who owns them. Staff shared the finding with commissioners Tuesday night in an update on the board's Sept. 1 decision to remove automated license plate readers from county-controlled property. The number of unpermitted cameras has climbed quickly. A county agenda report signed Sept. 10 said field checks had turned up three cameras at unpermitted locations. By Tuesday, staff said the count had reached at least 14, and the search is not finished. County commissioner James Clasby says the issue isn't as much about the cameras as who's receiving the data. Not knowing who they belong to, I think, is another issue. Perhaps that goes about the entirety of Flock camera reform, Clasby said. "There's the potential for non-law enforcement to have cameras out there, and I'm not okay with that. Because the county has no permit on file for those cameras, staff said it cannot identify an applicant to contact. Instead, the county is posting removal notices directly on the devices. "It's like a bright red notice that says you have 30 days to remove this. And we will also bag the cameras so they're not operable," said interim county administrator Mayte Santamaria. Staff said the county has not yet gone through its entire right-of-way and more unauthorized cameras may still be found. Staff is also double-checking some traffic signals that interact with state right-of-way, which could add a handful more. The agenda report says staff is comparing crowdsourced data from various sources against known locations to find unknown or unauthorized installations. See also: Florida boaters rescued after capsized vessel leaves them stranded in tree The unpermitted cameras are in addition to 52 devices the county previously authorized within its rights-of-way. Staff said all 52 had received revocation notices as of Monday, giving their owners 30 days to remove them. According to the report, county permit records indicate most of the authorized devices were installed on behalf of law enforcement agencies. The county shared its inventory with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, the Fort Pierce Police Department and the Port St. Lucie Police Department ahead of the notices. The report says that step was meant both to give the agencies advance notice and to let them review the data for accuracy. Staff also told commissioners there are no active applications for new devices under review. Commissioners voted 3-2 on Sept. 1 to stop issuing permits for Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers on county-owned or county-controlled property. The vote went beyond a state order that applies only to state highways. Commissioner James Clasby made the motion, which he said was about protecting residents' privacy. Commissioners Clasby, Lee and Lowry voted yes, and Chair Jamie Fowler and Commissioner Cathy Townsend voted no. The board's direction does not apply to license plate readers mounted in law enforcement vehicles or cameras on private property.

A 42-year-old travel MRI technician was arrested after Port St. Lucie police said a patient reported she was sexually assaulted while undergoing an MRI at HCA Florida St. Gabriel Cruz was arrested in Brevard County on the evening of Sept. 16 on a charge of sexual battery involving a physically helpless or incapacitated victim, a first-degree felony, police said. Wasana Chesler is a former patient of St. Lucie Hospital and couldn't believe the news. That's very horrible," Chesler said. "That's very sad." The investigation began Sept. 14 after hospital staff reported that a 64-year-old female patient said she had been sexually assaulted during an MRI the day before at the hospital, 1800 SE Tiffany Ave. Police said the woman had been admitted for medical treatment and was given medication before the MRI that left her significantly drowsy. Detectives identified Cruz as the technician assigned to the procedure. With the hospital’s assistance, investigators obtained video that police said showed Cruz leaving the MRI room after the patient and disposing of materials. See also: Amazon closes Port St. Lucie warehouse for major renovation, hundreds impacted by layoffs Those materials were recovered and tested, returning presumptive positive results for male semen, according to police. Cruz had worked at the hospital as a travel MRI technician since Aug. 24 and was hired through a third-party agency, police said. Monica Defoster said she's been to St. Lucie Hospital many times including on Thursday while visiting her husband. She calls the allegations disturbing. They should have more than one person in the MRI room," Defoster said. "You go to the hospital and don't expect something like that." The investigation remains active. Lucie Hospital has cooperated with investigators, police said. Lucie Hospital provided CBS12 News with the following statement: We do not tolerate behavior that jeopardizes the safety or security of our patients. When this serious allegation was reported to us, we contacted law enforcement and ended the individual’s assignment. We have assisted law enforcement throughout its investigation and remain focused on supporting our patient. A hospital spokesman told CBS12 no other complaints have been reported since Cruz stared working there late last month. Cruz's employer could not be reached for comment. He remains behind bars in Brevard County.

Health officials have issued a blue-green algae health alert for an area of Lake Okeechobee after water samples detected harmful toxins. The Florida Department of Health in Martin County said the alert covers the Lake Okeechobee NES135 area and was issued in response to samples collected Sept. The area is located on the north shore of the lake at J&S Fish Camp in Martin County. Residents and visitors should use caution in and around the lake, officials said. People should not drink, swim, wade, use personal watercraft or otherwise come into contact with water where a visible algae bloom is present. Health officials also advised people to keep pets and livestock away from affected water. Anyone who comes into contact with algae, discolored water or water with an unpleasant odor should wash their skin and clothing with soap and water, according to the department. Officials said contaminated water should not be used for cooking or washing dishes because boiling does not remove algae toxins. Blue-green algae are bacteria commonly found in Florida freshwater. Blooms can discolor water and create floating mats, scum, foam or paint-like material on the surface, sometimes with an unpleasant odor. The blooms can produce toxins that may harm people, pets and aquatic life. Children, older adults and people with weakened immune systems may be at risk even at low toxin concentrations and should avoid exposure, health officials said. RELATED: 'Influence campaign': Okeechobee County leaders want to change Lake O's narrative Officials said it is safe to eat fillets from healthy freshwater fish caught in lakes experiencing blooms if the fillets are rinsed with tap or bottled water, the guts are discarded and the fish is thoroughly cooked. People should not eat shellfish from waters with algae blooms. The Florida Department of Environmental Protection monitors reported blooms and collects samples for analysis. The public can report an algae bloom online at ReportAlgalBloom.com or call 1-855-305-3903 . Anyone who develops symptoms after exposure to a harmful algae bloom can call the Florida Poison Information Center at 800-222-1222 . Pet owners who believe an animal became ill after exposure should contact a veterinarian. For health questions about blue-green algae, call DOH-Martin at 772-221-4090 .

Lucie fulfillment center is closing Thursday for a major renovation, leaving hundreds of workers out of a job while others have transferred to different facilities. When Amazon filed its layoff notice in July, 494 employees were listed as affected. Since then, more than 200 workers have transferred to other Amazon locations, according to information provided to CBS12 News. Around 300 employees are expected to take severance as the Port St. Lucie facility shuts down. Local workforce organizations, including CareerSource Research Coast and the Economic Development Council of St. Lucie County, have spent recent months holding job fairs and helping affected workers connect with other employers. Lucie County Commissioner Cathy Townsend said the closure highlights the importance of attracting a wider range of businesses to the county. I think we need to be more strategic on the companies we want coming here, Townsend said. My focus would be more on small businesses. See also: CBS12 I-Team: Amendment 3 backers say tax relief could help Florida homeowners stay put The closure is expected to last until at least 2028. Amazon plans to invest about $200 million to renovate and expand the facility. Lucie EDC said the work will include advanced robotics and artificial intelligence capabilities, along with an additional 870,000 square feet. Amazon plans to reopen the facility in the second half of 2028 and hire more than 1,000 employees. Workers who were employed at the facility before the closure will be eligible for rehire when it reopens, according to the EDC. Amazon has said the closure is not expected to impact customers because operations will be handled by other facilities during the renovation.

Lucie Police say they used a dead man's own phone to text his alleged drug dealer and arrange a buy, an investigation that led to a search warrant, thousands in cash, guns and drugs found at the dealer's home. According to the arrest affidavit, officers responded to an apartment at 700 SE Collins Lane on September 13th for an overdose. They found 34-year-old Miqueias Oliveira Silva dead, with a bloody syringe and a bag of cocaine next to him. The affidavit says rigor mortis suggested Silva had been dead for about 24 hours. It’s destroying the community. It’s destroying the members of the community, said Magalys Koch, a substance abuse expert at Hibiscus Counseling. A neighbor who called 911 told police he last saw Silva getting out of the passenger side of a black SUV before going inside, according to the affidavit. Investigators say they went through Silva's phone and found months of text exchanges with a contact saved under the name Danilo Jaramillo, going back to August 17th. The affidavit says the messages followed a pattern, with Silva asking if Jaramillo was "available" and Jaramillo confirming before the two met up. Police say they used Silva's phone to text Jaramillo and arrange another deal. Jaramillo responded he could be there within the hour. Investigators say they followed Jaramillo's black Kia Telluride to Silva's apartment complex, then pulled him over. A K9 alerted to narcotics inside the vehicle. Investigators say they found a bag of fentanyl on the passenger seat, along with a large amount of cash. See also: Vero Beach animal hospital manager accused of reclaiming cats, abandoning them outside Detectives then obtained a search warrant for Jaramillo's home on SW Longfellow Road. According to a separate affidavit, investigators searched the master bedroom. They found three firearms a Smith & Wesson .40 caliber handgun, a Ruger LC9 and an AR-15 along with ammunition, digital scales, a written ledger, cocaine, marijuana and $17,715 in cash. Jaramillo's wife, Selina Jaramillo, was home with their children during the search. According to the affidavit, she told investigators she didn't know he was involved in drugs and said she'd last seen him with narcotics about eight months earlier. She said one of the firearms was hers, but that the rest, along with the drugs and cash, belonged to her husband. The affidavit says Jaramillo told police anything illegal in the home belonged to him, then asked for a lawyer before answering further questions. Because Jaramillo is a convicted felon, investigators charged him with three counts of possessing a firearm or ammunition as a felon. Police say body cameras were active throughout the search and the footage was submitted into evidence. Jaramillo, 43, faces multiple felony drug charges, including fentanyl trafficking, along with three felony weapons counts and a misdemeanor paraphernalia charge. He was booked into the St. Koch says oftentimes the pain is felt not just by the victims and dealers, but by the people around them. Many parents or family members feel guilty, like they didn't do enough or they couldn't. They say, "What could have been done differently?" So, they actually carry the guilt, Koch said. While state data points to a steady decline in overdose deaths since 2021, Koch says that addiction is still a rampant cycle. We're moving away from being in touch with who we are. We don't want to have any pain. We don't want to be bored. We want to be entertained. So these drugs come in, and who can compete with cocaine? CBS12 News has reached out to Port St. Lucie Police for comment and is working to confirm additional details.

The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office announced more than 50 arrests following a multi-agency, multi-day operation targeting human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county. Operation Late Checkout ran from Sept. 13 in Indian River County. The operation netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers, Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a press conference on Thursday. Flowers announced the results alongside a representative from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. “Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office, Seminole County Sheriff’s Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney’s Office,” Flowers said. The operation’s targeted goal was stopping human trafficking in the Indian River County area, the sheriff’s office said. During the operation, several victims were identified, and investigators said ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time. One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online. “Our team did a great job of getting him off the street,” Flowers said. Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation, the sheriff’s office said. Victims’ advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were also on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked. “We have many ongoing investigations as a result of this,” Flowers said. Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County. “We’ve never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot,” he said. FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county. “This operation shows that within our communities there are dangerous individuals committing heinous crimes who think they can get away with it,” Williams said. Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors. “Our work is far from done,” Williams said. “This operation requires a lot of resources and time. We cannot do this work alone, and our success depends on the great partnership and collaboration that you see today.” FDLE said it houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. A Vero Beach animal hospital manager was arrested after investigators said she reclaimed two cats from the Humane Society of Vero Beach and Indian River County, then abandoned them outdoors without care. Deanna Rae Wesley, 43, was arrested Sept. 15 on an active warrant charging her with two counts of animal abandonment, both first-degree misdemeanors, according to Indian River County court records. Animal Control investigators said Wesley, who works at Dr. Dan’s Animal Hospital , picked up two white-and-brown tabby cats from the Humane Society on Sept. Wesley reportedly told staff the cats were being returned to a caregiver, but she would not identify that person, the affidavit said. The next day, Animal Control received a complaint about a white-and-brown tabby cat crying at a resident’s front door. Investigators said the cat was taken to Animal Control, where its microchip and Humane Society staff confirmed it was one of the cats Wesley had picked up. An investigator said Wesley initially denied it was the same cat but acknowledged the matching microchip number. According to the affidavit, she declined to explain how the cat ended up loose at the home. The resident told investigators that a woman matching Wesley’s description, wearing a Dr. Dan’s T-shirt, spoke with her mother and warned her to watch out for Animal Control in the area. The woman allegedly called the cats colony cats, the affidavit said. See also: Amazon closes Port St. Lucie warehouse for major renovation, hundreds impacted by layoffs Animal Control recovered the second cat at the same residence Sept. Both cats were described as extremely friendly, with debris on their faces and chins. Investigators said the cats were not capable of surviving outdoors on their own and that no one was known to be caring for them. Health officials have issued a blue-green algae health alert for an area of Lake Okeechobee after water samples detected harmful toxins. The Florida Department of Health in Martin County said the alert covers the Lake Okeechobee NES135 area and was issued in response to samples collected Sept. The area is located on the north shore of the lake at J&S Fish Camp in Martin County. Residents and visitors should use caution in and around the lake, officials said. People should not drink, swim, wade, use personal watercraft or otherwise come into contact with water where a visible algae bloom is present. Health officials also advised people to keep pets and livestock away from affected water. Anyone who comes into contact with algae, discolored water or water with an unpleasant odor should wash their skin and clothing with soap and water, according to the department. Officials said contaminated water should not be used for cooking or washing dishes because boiling does not remove algae toxins. Blue-green algae are bacteria commonly found in Florida freshwater. Blooms can discolor water and create floating mats, scum, foam or paint-like material on the surface, sometimes with an unpleasant odor. The blooms can produce toxins that may harm people, pets and aquatic life. Children, older adults and people with weakened immune systems may be at risk even at low toxin concentrations and should avoid exposure, health officials said. RELATED: 'Influence campaign': Okeechobee County leaders want to change Lake O's narrative Officials said it is safe to eat fillets from healthy freshwater fish caught in lakes experiencing blooms if the fillets are rinsed with tap or bottled water, the guts are discarded and the fish is thoroughly cooked. People should not eat shellfish from waters with algae blooms. The Florida Department of Environmental Protection monitors reported blooms and collects samples for analysis. The public can report an algae bloom online at ReportAlgalBloom.com or call 1-855-305-3903 . Anyone who develops symptoms after exposure to a harmful algae bloom can call the Florida Poison Information Center at 800-222-1222 . Pet owners who believe an animal became ill after exposure should contact a veterinarian. For health questions about blue-green algae, call DOH-Martin at 772-221-4090 .

Martin County High School received another threat through the state's FortifyFL reporting system, the third bomb threat involving our campus this week, the school district said Friday afternoon. "I recognize that you have heard from me repeatedly this week regarding safety-related disruptions on our campus," Principal Lori Vogel said in a message to families. The latest threat referenced two specific buildings, requiring students and staff to be evacuated while law enforcement conducted a thorough search. Students and staff were relocated to other areas of campus during the response. On Monday, students and staff were evacuated after a bomb threat prompted a response from the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Eight days ago, students and staff were evacuated in the afternoon after a bomb threat was received via email, according to school officials. In a message sent to families, school officials said all buildings were being evacuated at the direction of law enforcement while authorities investigate the threat. Vogel noted the seriousness of the threats. "Every threat must be taken seriously," the principal said. "Each report generates a significant law enforcement response, disrupts instruction, displaces students and staff, and creates understandable concern throughout our school community. Unlike many situations that may require an emergency response, the behavior prompting these repeated disruptions is entirely avoidable. We need our families as partners in addressing this behavior. Please speak directly with your children about the seriousness and far-reaching impact of making or participating in a false threat." The message added: "What a student may view as a joke or a temporary way to avoid class can have widespread consequences for an entire campus and community. FortifyFL is an important safety resource. Information about submitting a report is available on our school's and the School District's websites. In opening the Buffalo Bills' new stadium, rookie coach Joe Brady was more interested in seeing his team put on a clinic rather than a show.Turns out, Brady got to see both in a 41-31 victory over the Detroit Lions on Thursday night in the Bills' first regular-season game at Highmark Stadium.Fireworks. And a win.“The atmosphere was incredible,” Brady said. “It was the game Buffalo deserved.”The 41 points were the third-most by a team in its regular-season stadium debut, behind only Dallas, which scored 44 in its first game at Texas Stadium in 1971, and Miami scoring 42 in its first outing at Joe Robbie Stadium in 1987.Josh Allen accounted for five touchdowns, including the first one, by scoring on a 1-yard run six minutes in. A sell-out crowd arrived early, and about 1,000 fans still lingered long after the final horn in cheering on Allen and left tackle Dion Dawkins as they were being interviewed at the Prime TV booth along the sideline.Among those on hand was former Bills quarterback-turned-broadcaster Ryan Fitzpatrick. He opened the day by throwing passes across the international border — from one boat to another on the Niagara River — to former Bills receiver Stevie Johnson.And the Bills honored their cross-border fanbase by having both the U.S. and Canadian anthems performed with both countries’ flags displayed on the field.The Toronto musical group Barenaked Ladies was greeted by a loud cheer before singing “O, Canada.” They were followed by Hawaiian-born actress and singer Auli’i Cravalho performing “The Star-Spangled Banner.” U.S. pop group OneRepublic also performed at halftime, while set up on a platform in the stands at the north end of the field.RELATED STORY | Chicago Bears could merge 2 sites for potential stadium in northwest Indiana“It was crazy. I don’t really get starstruck, but there was a few times I looked up like, this is crazy,” defensive tackle Deone Walker said.The festivities began with an elaborate light show with fans wearing bracelets that blinked, followed by a fireworks display as the Bills offensive starters were introduced, with Allen greeted by a roar and chants of “M-V-P! M-V-P!”And the Bills even rolled out a new green grass carpet by choosing to resod the entire field ahead of schedule following their preseason finale against Pittsburgh on Aug. They did so after the original turf, which had been laid down in October, showed signs of wear and tear, and with large divots having to be replaced during two preseason games and two practices.Bills players indicated after practicing in the stadium on Tuesday that the grass felt firmer, and noticed a larger infill of sand. That was evident in pregame warmups when clumps of sand came up when players made hard cuts on the field.During the opening drive, an on-field official was spotted having to tamp down a clump of grass that came up at the 30.Otherwise, there were few other noticeable issues.“I thought it held up extremely well tonight,” Allen said.The only other apparent hiccup occurred when the teams lined up prematurely for the opening kickoff, and then stayed in formation for several minutes during a commercial break.The field was painted for the first time, with the word “BILLS” in large white block letters featured prominently in both end zones over red-painted grass. The team’s charging Buffalo logo was also added at midfield.The new stadium has a capacity of just over 60,000, about 12,000 less than the old facility, which now lies in rubble across the street.RELATED STORY | Lakers ownership drama: Jeanie Buss challenges siblings’ sale planWhat’s different is the layout, with the new facility’s seating structure built more vertically in placing viewers more on top of the action. The new building also features a canopy, which helps project crowd noise directly onto the field.“It was great. Everything was awesome,” edge rusher Greg Rousseau said, before crediting the team’s owner Terry Pegula. “Shout out Pegula for an amazing stadium.”

Two men were arrested after a road rage incident escalated into a shooting near SW California Boulevard and SW Brevity Terrace on Sept. 17, 2026, at approximately 6:30 p.m., according to the Port St. Investigators determined the incident began as a misunderstanding between two drivers. One driver believed he was being followed after changing lanes and merging from SW Crosstown Parkway, where the vehicles had crossed paths, and one driver thought the other had cut him off. However, police said the investigation revealed there was no intentional following. One of the drivers, identified as 57-year-old Tylon Kukielka, was traveling with his girlfriend to her home after visiting a local restaurant. The other driver, identified as 41-year-old Dean Plotts, happened to be traveling in the same direction and onto the same streets. As the vehicles continued, the situation escalated into a physical confrontation near SW Brevity Terrace. During the altercation, Kukielka fired a handgun, striking Plotts twice. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputy who was in the area traveling on SW California Boulevard observed the incident and detained Kukielka. Plotts sustained gunshot wounds to his left wrist and legs and was transported to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Kukielka was also transported for medical evaluation. Detectives responded to the scene and collected evidence, including shell casings, surveillance video, dash cam footage, and other physical evidence. Based on the evidence collected, witness information, video footage, and statements obtained during the investigation, detectives determined there was probable cause to charge Kukielka with attempted homicide – murder, dangerous depraved without premeditation, a first-degree felony under Florida Statute 782.04(2). Detectives also determined there was probable cause to charge Plotts with burglary with assault or battery, a felony under Florida Statute 810.02(2)(a). Both men were taken into custody in connection with the investigation, which remains ongoing. All defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in a court of law. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis has signed a death warrant for 77-year-old William Reaves Jr., the man convicted of murdering Indian River County Sheriff's Deputy Richard Raczkoski in 1986. The execution is scheduled for Tuesday, Oct. 20, at 6 p.m.Reaves was convicted of murdereing Raczkoski on Sept. 23, 1986, after a confrontation at a convenience store.Deputy Raczkoski had responded to a 911 call at the store when he encountered Reaves. During a conversation between the two, a gun fell from Reaves's shorts. Deputy Raczkoski placed his knee on the weapon. Reaves then pushed the deputy away, grabbed the gun and pointed it at Deputy Raczkoski's face.As Deputy Raczkoski attempted to draw his own weapon, Reaves said, "I wouldn't do that if I were you." The deputy backed away, turned, and ran. Reaves fired seven rounds, striking Deputy Raczkoski four times.Reaves was tried in the 19th Judicial Circuit in Indian River County. On direct appeal, the Florida Supreme Court reversed the initial conviction and remanded the case for a new trial. On remand, Reaves was again convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death on March 6, 1992, in Vero Beach.The Florida Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and death sentence on April 7, 1994. The United States Supreme Court denied Reaves's petition for a writ of certiorari on Nov. 7, 1994.Reaves pursued numerous postconviction challenges in both state and federal courts over the following decades.In 2015, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida granted Reaves's federal petition for a writ of habeas corpus. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit overturned that ruling and ordered that the petition be denied.Additional postconviction motions and petitions were subsequently denied, and those denials were affirmed on appeal. Executive clemency was also considered and denied.Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, in his letter recommending the warrant, wrote that "the record is legally sufficient to support the issuance of a death warrant," and confirmed that "there are no stays of execution issued by any court of competent jurisdiction in this cause."The execution is scheduled to take place at Florida State Prison in Raiford. If carried out as scheduled, it will come 40 years after the murder of Deputy Raczkoski.

Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks, Frank Frangella still carries the memories of what he witnessed at Ground Zero. The Martin County School District's Director of Safety & Security was a New York City Police Department officer when terrorists struck the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001.WATCH BELOW:"It's always there and there are always little things that remind you of what happened," Frangella said from his office, surrounded by photos, statues and a book of memories honoring those lost in the attacks.Frangella was asleep after working the midnight shift when his wife woke him with news that would change his life forever."I was actually asleep when the first plane hit and my wife woke me up and she goes – a plane just hit the World Trade Center," Frangella recalled. "There was a big hole in that building and I knew right away what that was, so I just started dressing."The weather that morning remains etched in his memory. "The one thing I remember from that day, soon as I walked out of the house – it was the most beautiful day in the world. There wasn't a cloud in the sky, and I'm thinking to myself driving to where I was going – how can this happen on such a beautiful day."Initially assigned to help intake victims at a Staten Island triage area, Frangella waited for hours as no injured survivors arrived. "It was like what's happening, you know. We're not getting any information."With communication systems failing, Frangella and fellow officers decided to take a boat directly to Ground Zero. What they found defied comprehension."By that time, both buildings were down. And I mean - it looked like a war zone," he said. "It was literally a pile, and it was huge."The scale of destruction was unlike anything Frangella had ever seen. "You figure two of the largest buildings in Manhattan, you didn't see a desk. Nothing that resembled an office building," he said. "Everything was pulverized."SPECIAL COVERAGE: Remembering 9/11What began as a rescue mission quickly became a recovery operation, according to Frangella. "Everybody that was down there was doing it because they wanted to save lives, and then we found out pretty quickly on that there was no lives to save, and it was a recovery mission more than anything else."Despite their efforts, Frangella's team did not find any survivors.The emotional toll of those days followed Frangella home to his family. "A few weeks later, I remember sitting home and it all hit. I just started crying and I don't even know why I was crying," he said.The dust-covered uniforms from Ground Zero created an unexpected memorial in the Frangella household. "We had a washing machine in the basement that she was washing all my clothing with and how many souls were in that wash. So, it was almost like a shrine in my house. We never used it again after 9/11 because it was like – it just felt wrong to use it."Today, Frangella applies his experience from that tragic day to his role protecting Martin County's school children. He often shares his story with students, creating powerful moments of connection."This little girl about this big walks over to me and she says -- can I hug you? When that little girl came over, there wasn't a dry eye in the house. I mean everybody started crying and she just said… thank you. It was the most amazing thing in the world," Frangella said.Despite his role in the response efforts, Frangella has never visited the 9/11 Memorial and Museum. "I was there when it happened. I don't need to relive it again," he said.As the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks approaches, first responders like Frangella continue processing their experiences while serving their communities in new ways. His transition from protecting New York City to safeguarding Martin County schools demonstrates how the impact of that day continues to shape public service careers across the country.Twenty-five years later, Frangella honors not just his own experience, but that of every person who responded that day. The Martin County Commission approved a zoning compromise for land in Hobe Sound, but the 3-2 vote has left some residents and at least one commissioner with lingering concerns about what could be built there.Commissioners voted to rezone a property along Southeast Powerline Avenue to limited-industrial, stepping back from a general industrial designation that drew pushback from nearby residents. The property has long been slated for some form of industrial use, but the county said the existing zoning was outdated and due for an update.WATCH: Hobe Sound zoning compromise raises data center concernsResidents who spoke at the Tuesday commission meeting said their primary concern was protecting the character of the community.Steve Addison said he has lived in the area since 1969."Our biggest concern was preserving our quality of life. We don't have a lot of industry and a lot of noise," Addison said.Other residents echoed concerns about the scope of the original rezoning proposal."I understand that Martin County has to plan for the future but I also believe that growth needs to be compatible with the community that already exists," Kim Call, a resident, said."We're concerned about the permanence of a GI classification which we believe is too broad and too open-ended," Patrick McDonough, a Hobe Sound resident and Eaglewood Community HOA president, said.After hearing from residents, the property owner offered to accept the less-intensive classification."To cooperate and show if that's what the neighbors feel is more appropriate and that would be a better use then we are willing to accept the light industrial," Bob Reins, a land-use attorney with Gunster law firm, said.Despite the compromise, Commissioner Blake Capps voted against the rezoning, citing concerns about the potential for a data center on the site."Who knows where this is really going in the future and to approve a zoning for this property that allows a data center. Any proposal exceeding 100,000 square feet would require board approval.In speaking with residents, WPTV'S Cassandra Garcia learned not everyone was happy with the outcome.
