hero.headline: Martin County approves limited-industrial zoning for Powerline Avenue site in Hobe Sound
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted 3-2 Tuesday to rezone property along Southeast Powerline Avenue in Hobe Sound to limited-industrial, stepping back from a general industrial designation that drew pushback from nearby residents. Commissioner Blake Capps voted against the rezoning, citing concerns about the potential for a data center on the site, and the county confirmed any proposal exceeding 100,000 square feet would require board approval.

The property has long been slated for some form of industrial use, but the county said the existing zoning was outdated and due for an update. Residents who spoke at the commission meeting said their primary concern was protecting the character of the community.

Steve Addison said he has lived in the area since 1969. "Our biggest concern was preserving our quality of life. We don't have a lot of industry and a lot of noise," Addison said. Kim Call said she believes growth needs to be compatible with the community that already exists. Patrick McDonough, a Hobe Sound resident and Eaglewood Community HOA president, said residents were concerned about the permanence of a general industrial classification which they believe is too broad and too open-ended.

After hearing from residents, the property owner offered to accept the less-intensive classification. "To cooperate and show if that's what the neighbors feel is more appropriate and that would be a better use then we are willing to accept the light industrial," Bob Reins, a land-use attorney with Gunster law firm, said.

Capps said he was not comfortable approving zoning for the property that allows a data center. "Who knows where this is really going in the future and to approve a zoning for this property that allows a data center. I'm not into that," Capps said. The county said there are no plans for a data center at the site.

Addison said he felt the outcome was the right move. "I don't want to see over development, but I also don't want to be that guy that doesn't understand land-use and doesn't understand property rights," Addison said. "I feel like it was a win win for the both of us."

hero.headline: Jolly proposes AI data center moratorium; Donalds warns freeze would drive investment from Florida
hero.body:
Florida's gubernatorial candidates have drawn a sharp line over artificial intelligence infrastructure, with Democrat David Jolly proposing a one-year moratorium on new data centers and Republican Byron Donalds warning that a statewide freeze could drive investment elsewhere.

Jolly, in a Sept. 13 interview with CBS Miami, said Florida needs more time to assess the effects on communities and natural resources. During a Tallahassee stop, he framed the proposal as a response to residents' concerns about water use, electricity costs and local control as communities weigh new facilities ahead of November's gubernatorial vote.

"We don't need data centers in the state of Florida at all, at all, at all," Jolly told CBS Miami. His campaign announced Sept. 14 that he would visit Northern Virginia's Data Center Alley this week to meet residents who say nearby facilities have disrupted their lives with persistent noise, air quality issues and other effects. Democrats launched a "Data Center Donalds" tour Tuesday in Pinellas County, with agriculture commissioner nominee Joey Mendoza Atkins and state House candidate Bryan Beckman joining residents at the site of a previously proposed data center.

Donalds argues Florida can protect communities while remaining open to infrastructure businesses need. "Capital goes where it's valued," he said in an August interview, warning that talk of bans and moratoriums could signal Florida is not the place to invest. "But you can't build for your life if you don't have a high-paying job. And you're not going to have a high-paying job if you don't have companies who invest in your state," Donalds said. Last week, Donalds described AI as a force multiplier, comparing its potential to the internet and personal computers. He supports keeping facilities away from homes and using cooling technology that conserves water, and said local governments should retain control over whether projects are built.

A July survey from the University of North Florida's Public Opinion Research Lab found 68% of likely Florida midterm voters opposed an AI data center in their local area, while 28% supported one. The poll surveyed 848 likely voters July 8–17. Voters were evenly divided on the general increase in AI use, with 49% supporting it and 49% opposing it.

Florida adopted new rules for large data centers when Ron DeSantis signed SB 484 in May. The law requires electricity rate structures designed to ensure large customers pay their own service costs, preserves local planning and land-use authority, and establishes water-permitting requirements for large data centers. It also calls for an independent study of their economic, environmental and public-health effects. Jolly argues paying for utilities does not resolve broader concerns. cards.headline: Florida ranks 8th most expensive in US for grocery essentials
cards.teaser: Florida shoppers pay $134.35 for a basket of 30 essential grocery items, about $2 more than the national average, according to a new study by Self Financial. Local shoppers say they cope with rising prices through couponing, bulk buying, and adjusting family meals.
cards.body:
Florida shoppers pay $134.35 for a basket of 30 essential grocery items, about $2 more than the national average, according to a new study by Self Financial. The analysis compared 30 essential grocery items, including meat, milk, eggs and produce, and found Florida ranks eighth most expensive in the country for the cost of essentials.

Local shoppers say they feel the impact every time they head to the store. Elaine Capute said looking for deals at the grocery store is a full-time job. "I go online for the Publix ad. I clip all the digital coupons because you never know what you're going to buy," Capute said. "I don't know what people do that work full time, because it really takes up a lot of my time, but we're retired, and I do what I have to do."

Retired chef Monte Schrier said his go-to strategy is shopping at a wholesaler, where he gets deals as a member. He showed his last receipt, where 40 pounds of bulk chicken breasts cost just $1.39 a pound. "Clean it, cut it, cryo-vac it and freeze it. A lot of people don't like to do that. They don't like to freeze stuff, but if you want to pay $6 a pound every time," Schrier said. Schrier said he also shops around, hitting two or three stores and getting the best deals at each.

Shopper Betty Magar said the strategy is planning ahead. "I eat for that week, what's on sale or what's a BOGO," Magar said. Shopper Bryce Hipp said with a fourth child on the way, the priority is making sure his kids have plenty. "Take a look at what we eat versus what our kids eat. We want our kids to not go without anything. Sometimes we might dial back what we might want," Hipp said.

Food prices continue to fluctuate. Uncooked turkey and other poultry are up 11.5% in the past year, and instant coffee is up 11%. Egg prices are down 23% over the past year.

hero.headline: Martin County approves limited-industrial zoning for Hobe Sound Powerline Avenue property in 3-2 vote
hero.body:
The Martin County Commission voted 3-2 Tuesday to approve limited-industrial zoning for a property along Southeast Powerline Avenue in Hobe Sound, stepping back from a general industrial designation that drew opposition from nearby residents. The approval leaves lingering concerns among some residents and Commissioner Blake Capps about the potential for a data center at the site, though the county requires board approval for any future project exceeding 100,000 square feet.

The property owner offered to accept the less-intensive limited-industrial classification after hearing from residents at the meeting. Bob Reins, a land-use attorney with Gunster law firm, said the property owner agreed to cooperate with neighbors who felt the designation would be more appropriate.

Capps voted against the rezoning despite the compromise, citing concerns about what could be built on the site. "Who knows where this is really going in the future and to approve a zoning for this property that allows a data center. I'm not into that," Capps said. The county said there are no plans for a data center at the site.

Residents who spoke at the commission meeting said their primary concern was protecting the character of the community. Steve Addison, who has lived in the area since 1969, said the biggest concern was preserving quality of life in an area without much industry and noise. Kim Call, a resident, said growth needs to be compatible with the community that already exists. Patrick McDonough, a Hobe Sound resident and Eaglewood Community HOA president, said residents were concerned about the permanence of a general industrial classification which would be too broad and open-ended.

The property has long been slated for some form of industrial use, but the county said the existing zoning was outdated and due for an update. Addison said he felt the outcome was a win for both sides. "I don't want to see over development, but I also don't want to be that guy that doesn't understand land-use and doesn't understand property rights," Addison said.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce commissioners grant King's Landing developers six-month extension
hero.body:
Fort Pierce city commissioners voted 3-2 Monday night to grant developers of the King's Landing project a six-month extension to raise $15 million for the long-delayed development near the downtown marina.

The extension gives Live Oak Holdings 180 days to secure funding for a hotel that is part of the mixed-use development. The multi-million-dollar project is expected to include a Marriott hotel, restaurant, residential units, retail space, and a parking garage.

Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky expressed frustration with the project's history and made a motion to terminate the development agreement, but that motion failed. Dzadovsky said the project has faced delays for seven years.

"Well, it's been seven years. We should be well past this process. I was disappointed in the outcome for sure," Dzadovsky said.

Current developer Bill Ware with Live Oak Holdings attended the meeting and told commissioners he should not be held accountable for delays that occurred before his company was approved in a third amendment in April 2025.

"I respectfully request that we not be held captive or accountable for this ten-year-plus period of time and prior to Live Oak being approved in the April of 2025 third amendment," Ware said.

Ware said he will continue monthly email updates and quarterly updates.

Officials agreed to move forward but instructed the developers to formally document their default. Michael Broderick said the document must address the city's concerns or it will not be approved.

Dzadovsky said he is not optimistic the deadline will be met.

"Given the seven years' experience, I think six months from now we'll be back to where we started today, last night," Dzadovsky said.

I was disappointed in the outcome for sure," Dzadovsky said. During Monday night's city commission meeting, Dzadovsky made a motion to terminate the development agreement, but the motion failed. Current developer Bill Ware with Live Oak Holdings also attended Monday night's city commission meeting. However, the project has faced several delays over the years. hero.headline: Jolly proposes data center moratorium; Donalds warns freeze could drive investment from Florida
hero.body:
Florida's gubernatorial candidates have turned artificial intelligence infrastructure into a campaign battleground, with Democrat David Jolly proposing a one-year moratorium on new data centers and Republican Byron Donalds warning that a statewide freeze could drive investment elsewhere. The clash puts water consumption, electricity costs and local land-use control at the center of debate as voters prepare to choose the state's next governor in November.

Jolly told CBS Miami in a Sept. 13 interview that Florida does not need data centers at all and should pause new development to assess effects on communities and natural resources. His campaign announced Sept. 14 that he would visit Northern Virginia's Data Center Alley this week to meet residents who say nearby facilities have disrupted their lives with persistent noise, air quality problems and other development impacts. During a Tallahassee stop, Jolly framed the proposal as a response to residents' concerns, saying leaders need to listen and follow public opinion.

Donalds argues Florida can protect communities while remaining open to infrastructure businesses need. He said in an August interview that capital goes where it is valued and that talk of bans and moratoriums could signal Florida is not the place to invest. He supports keeping facilities away from homes and using cooling technology that conserves water, including systems that recirculate water or use air cooling. Last week, Donalds described AI as a force multiplier comparable to the internet and personal computers. He said local governments should retain control over whether projects are built, stating that if a local government does not want to build it, they will not build it.

Democrats launched their Data Center Donalds tour Tuesday in Pinellas County, accusing Donalds of putting industry donors ahead of communities. Agriculture commissioner nominee Joey Mendoza Atkins and state House candidate Bryan Beckman joined residents at the site of a previously proposed data center. A July survey from the University of North Florida's Public Opinion Research Lab found 68% of likely Florida midterm voters opposed an AI data center in their local area, while 28% supported one. The same survey found voters evenly divided on the general increase in AI use, with 49% supporting it and 49% opposing it. The poll surveyed 848 likely voters July 8-17.

Ron DeSantis signed SB 484 in May establishing new rules for large data centers. The law requires electricity rate structures designed to ensure large customers pay their own service costs, preserves local planning and land-use authority, establishes water-permitting requirements for large data centers, and calls for an independent study of their economic, environmental and public-health effects. Jolly argues paying for utilities does not resolve broader concerns, saying Donalds is basically saying companies can plunder natural resources as long as they pay their own way. Donalds countered in August that leadership requires more than following public opinion, saying it is easy to listen to what everybody is saying and follow the polling, but that is not leadership.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce grants King's Landing developers fifth extension despite motion to terminate deal
hero.body:
Fort Pierce city commissioners voted 3-2 Monday night to grant developers of the King's Landing project a six-month extension to raise $15 million for the long-delayed mixed-use development near the downtown marina. The vote came after Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky made a motion to terminate the development agreement, which failed. Dzadovsky expressed frustration with the project's timeline, saying he was disappointed in the outcome. "Well, it's been seven years. We should be well past this process. I was disappointed in the outcome for sure," he said.

The extension gives Live Oak Holdings 180 days to secure funding for a hotel that is part of the project. Current developer Bill Ware attended the commission meeting and said he would continue providing updates. "I will continue my monthly email updates, but I'll also continue my monthly quarterly updates," Ware said. The multi-million-dollar project is expected to include a Marriott hotel, restaurant, residential units, retail space, and a parking garage. However, the project has faced several delays over the years.

Ware asked commissioners not to hold Live Oak accountable for delays that occurred before the company was approved in an April 2025 third amendment to the development agreement. "I respectfully request that we not be held captive or accountable for this ten-year-plus period of time and prior to Live Oak being approved in the April of 2025 third amendment," Ware said. The commissioners agreed to move forward but instructed the developers to formally document their default.

Commissioner Michael Broderick said the city's concerns must be addressed in that document or it will not be approved. "Our concerns need to be addressed in that document, or it's not going to get approved," Broderick said. Dzadovsky said he is not optimistic the extension will change the outcome. "Given the seven years' experience, I think six months from now we'll be back to where we started today, last night," he said. The developers now have 180 days to secure the funding and move the project forward.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce commissioners extend Kings Landing hotel funding deadline 180 days
hero.body:
Fort Pierce city commissioners voted 3-2 Monday to give developers of the Kings Landing development 180 days to find $15 million in funding for the hotel portion of the project. Developers Live Oak and Main Sail say the Marriott hotel will now cost around $65 million, $15 million more than previously planned.

The extension comes after developers missed a July 15 deadline to secure the funding. Earlier this summer, developers asked the city for the funds through a loan or grant, but were denied. Jon Collier with Main Sail said they will now look to secure the funds privately.

Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky voted against the extension. Dzadovsky said another amendment would continue to weaken the city's position and make it more difficult to get the property back. Commissioner Michael Broderick, who voted for the extension, said taking back the property, currently owned by Audubon Development, would be costly and lead to litigation. Broderick said the city has 30 days to draft a new amendment with developers, after which the six-month countdown will begin. Broderick said if developers fail to find the money in time, he will make the motion to terminate the deal.

Jon Nolli, who owns the Funky Cuda and other businesses in Fort Pierce and has a deposit on space in the Kings Landing development for a beer garden and deli, said he is cautiously watching the situation unfold. Nolli said he is still concerned about further delays. A representative from Live Oak said the development team remains committed. The representative said with millions of dollars invested thus far and an enormous amount of time, the team is extremely motivated to see the project through to a successful completion.

hero.headline: Liquor theft suspect led Martin County deputies on high-speed chase into Palm Beach County
hero.body:
A 24-year-old man is facing charges after allegedly stealing liquor from a Publix and leading deputies on a chase from Martin County into Palm Beach County.

Derwyn Edwards stole several bottles of liquor from a Publix before deputies attempted to stop him, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Edwards refused to pull over when a deputy caught up with his vehicle. Video from the pursuit shows him speeding, running red lights and coming dangerously close to other drivers on the road, authorities said.

Sheriff's office air crews tracked Edwards as he continued driving into Palm Beach County. The chase ended when Edwards was taken into custody. He is now charged with theft and fleeing police.

hero.headline: Amazon Port St. Lucie workers receive final paychecks Sept. 17 as facility begins two-year renovation
hero.body:
Amazon workers at the Port St. Lucie fulfillment center will receive their final paychecks Sept. 17 as the facility begins a two-year renovation. The center closed Sept. 6, and affected workers have continued to be paid until their employment is officially terminated.

Since the closure was announced in May, a majority of employees have found new work by the time the closure took place, according to Wicker Perlis, spokesperson for the St. Lucie County Economic Development Council. Many employees successfully transferred to other Amazon locations or found work with new employers.

The St. Lucie County Economic Development Council partnered with CareerSource Research Coast and local businesses to assist workers in finding new jobs. CareerSource organized hiring events and job assistance programs specifically for the displaced Amazon employees, bringing in companies such as Walmart, CVS and Pursuit Aero to connect with workers. Walmart interviewed dozens of employees and hired 25. Import Mex hired 12 workers and is considering others for future openings, while CVS Distribution hired two.

Four reemployment sessions were held, reaching over 100 affected workers with information on job placement services, training programs and other resources. The timing of new employers and expanding businesses helped create options for many of the people looking for their next paycheck, county officials said. Amazon has announced that the renovated facility is expected to reopen in 2028 with about 1,000 employees.

"With millions of dollars invested thus far and an enormous amount of time, we're extremely motivated to see this through to a successful completion," the representative said. The extension comes after developers missed a July 15 deadline to secure the funding for the project. Fort Pierce Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky voted against the extension. "My opinion, based on the legal review of this, is that we need to stop now. Because if we do another amendment, it continues to weaken us and makes it more difficult to get the property back," Dzadovsky said. On Tuesday, WPTV sat down with Commissioner Michael Broderick, who voted for the extension. Broderick said taking back the property — currently owned by Audubon Development — would be costly and lead to litigation. "Everybody's going to be suing everybody. It's like having three fighters in the same ring, and they're all going to come out swinging at each other," Broderick said. Broderick said the city has 30 days to draft a new amendment with developers, after which the six-month countdown will begin. When asked what happens if developers fail to find the money in time, Broderick was direct. "I'm going to kick them to the curb. I'll make the motion to terminate the deal," Broderick said. Jon Nolli, who owns the Funky Cuda and other businesses in Fort Pierce and has a deposit on space in the Kings Landing development for a beer garden and deli, said he is cautiously watching the situation unfold. "If this is really what it takes and they can find the money to be able to do this, great. Then we can get moving forward," Nolli said. Nolli said he is still concerned about further delays. "If this is just another step extending it along, that's going to be pretty tough on everybody," Nolli said. hero.headline: St. Lucie County finds 14 unpermitted license plate readers during sweep, with more checks ahead
hero.body:
St. Lucie County has found at least 14 license plate reader cameras installed on county rights-of-way without permits, and officials say they do not know who owns them. The discovery comes as the county carries out its decision to remove all automated license plate readers from county-controlled property, a directive commissioners approved Sept. 1.

County staff shared the finding with commissioners Tuesday night. The number of unpermitted cameras has climbed quickly from an initial tally. A county agenda report signed Sept. 10 said field checks had turned up three cameras at unpermitted locations. By Tuesday, staff said the count had reached at least 14. The search is not finished. Staff said the county has not yet gone through its entire right-of-way and more unauthorized cameras may still be found. Staff is also double-checking some traffic signals that interact with state right-of-way, which could add a handful more.

Because the county has no permit on file for the 14 cameras, staff said it cannot identify an applicant to contact. Instead, the county is posting removal notices directly on the devices. Interim county administrator Mayte Santamaria said the notices are bright red and state that owners have 30 days to remove the cameras. Staff is also bagging the cameras so they are not operable. The agenda report says staff is comparing crowdsourced data from various sources against known locations to find unknown or unauthorized installations.

The unpermitted cameras are in addition to 52 devices the county previously authorized within its rights-of-way. Staff said all 52 had received revocation notices as of Monday, giving their owners 30 days to remove them. According to the report, county permit records indicate most of the authorized devices were installed on behalf of law enforcement agencies. The county shared its inventory with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, the Fort Pierce Police Department and the Port St. Lucie Police Department ahead of the notices. Staff also told commissioners there are no active applications for new devices under review.

Commissioners voted 3-2 on Sept. 1 to stop issuing permits for Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers on county-owned or county-controlled property. Commissioner James Clasby made the motion, which he said was about protecting residents' privacy. Commissioners Clasby, Lee and Lowry voted yes. Chair Jamie Fowler and Commissioner Cathy Townsend voted no. The board's direction does not apply to license plate readers mounted in law enforcement vehicles or cameras on private property.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie bus stop complaint prompts district route change on Paar Drive
cards.teaser: St. Lucie Public Schools changed a bus route near Paar Drive after a Port St. Lucie mother raised safety concerns about students walking on a roadway without sidewalks, though the district maintains the original stop remains appropriate.
cards.body:
St. Lucie Public Schools altered a bus route near Paar Drive after a Port St. Lucie mother publicly complained about students walking along a roadway with no sidewalk, though the district said the original bus stop remains appropriate for student use.

Belinda Green raised concerns about a bus stop at Paar Drive and Winslow Street and posted a video on TikTok showing the area. Green said students are forced to walk along portions of Paar Drive where there is no sidewalk and limited space next to the road. She suggested the district split the stop to create an additional stop at Paar Drive and Jarmer Road to reduce the distance students walk along the roadway and prevent them from crossing the street after the bus has left.

The district's transportation department reviewed all routes and bus stops in the area and determined the existing stops are appropriate for student use. But after WPTV brought Green's concerns to the district, officials made a route change nearby to reduce the need for students to cross the road. The district said students who do need to cross should do so under the direction of the bus driver and with the bus's safety control devices.

Green said her biggest concern is the limited space available for students walking along Paar Drive. She pointed to the white line marking the edge of the car lane and said that space should not be used by pedestrians. Green said addressing potential safety concerns now is better than waiting for a serious incident.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce grants King's Landing developers 180 days to raise $15 million after 3-2 vote
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce city commissioners voted 3-2 Monday night to give King's Landing developers six more months to secure $15 million for the long-delayed mixed-use project near the downtown marina.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce city commissioners voted 3-2 Monday night to give King's Landing developers six more months to secure $15 million for the long-delayed mixed-use project near the downtown marina. Developers now have 180 days to raise the funding for a hotel that is part of the development.

Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky made a motion to terminate the development agreement during the meeting, but the motion failed. Dzadovsky expressed frustration with the seven-year delay.

"Well, it's been seven years. We should be well past this process. I was disappointed in the outcome for sure," Dzadovsky said.

Bill Ware, the current developer with Live Oak Holdings, attended the meeting. Ware told commissioners he would continue monthly and quarterly email updates.

"I respectfully request that we not be held captive or accountable for this ten-year-plus period of time and prior to Live Oak being approved in the April of 2025 third amendment," Ware said.

The multi-million-dollar project is expected to include a Marriott hotel, restaurant, residential units, retail space, and a parking garage. The project has faced several delays over the years.

Commissioners agreed to move forward but instructed developers to formally document their default. Commissioner Michael Broderick said the commission's concerns need to be addressed in that document or it will not get approved.

Dzadovsky remained skeptical about the extension.

"Given the seven years' experience, I think six months from now we'll be back to where we started today, last night," Dzadovsky said.

Current developer Bill Ware with Live Oak Holdings also attended Monday night's city commission meeting. "I will continue my monthly email updates, but I'll also continue my monthly quarterly updates," Ware said. However, the project has faced several delays over the years. hero.headline: Lake Worth man charged after fleeing Martin County deputies at 80+ mph, tracked by helicopter
hero.teaser: Derwyn Don Edwards, 24, faces charges after allegedly stealing liquor from a Publix in Martin County and leading deputies on a reckless flight into Palm Beach County before being captured with the help of the Martin County Sheriff's Office helicopter.
hero.body:
A 24-year-old Lake Worth man faces charges after allegedly stealing liquor from a Martin County store and fleeing from deputies at speeds exceeding 80 mph before being tracked by helicopter and taken into custody in Palm Beach County. Derwyn Don Edwards was arrested and charged with reckless fleeing and eluding and petit theft. He is being held at the Martin County Jail.

According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, Edwards entered the Publix liquor store at 6805 SE Federal Highway around 11:24 a.m. and stole multiple bottles of liquor. The retailer provided deputies with a description of Edwards and the vehicle he was driving.

A deputy located the vehicle near SE Dominica Terrace and Federal Highway and attempted a traffic stop, but authorities said Edwards failed to stop and continued driving recklessly. Because the incident did not meet the agency's pursuit-policy criteria, the deputy turned off emergency lights and siren and disengaged. Deputies said Edwards nevertheless continued driving dangerously, at times exceeding 80 mph, running red lights and endangering the public before heading south on Interstate 95.

MCSO Air 1 then located the vehicle and monitored it from above, guiding deputies as Edwards entered Palm Beach County without a ground pursuit. Authorities said Edwards eventually parked and attempted to hide. Air 1 directed an unmarked unit to his location, and he was taken into custody with assistance from the Florida Highway Patrol.

cards.headline: South Fork High School expands co-teaching model with Martin County planning elementary rollout
cards.teaser: Kevin Kobold teaches geometry with a partner at South Fork High School in Stuart as part of a co-teaching model now in its second year at the school. District officials say the approach will soon be introduced in Martin County elementary schools.
cards.body:
Kevin Kobold teaches geometry with a partner at South Fork High School in Stuart as part of a co-teaching model now in its second year at the school. District officials say the approach will soon be introduced in Martin County elementary schools.

The co-teaching model places two instructors in the same classroom. Kobold said a typical class has 28 to 29 students. With two teachers splitting the room, the ratio becomes roughly 15 students to one teacher, allowing more individual attention for struggling students.

"I'm helping take a lot off her weight that she doesn't have to be up there instructing from bell to bell every class. I can be doing the same thing too. So, getting to know your co-teacher and knowing your role in the classroom, I think, is key there," Kobold said.

Kobold focuses on making geometry lessons interactive rather than relying on note-taking. He uses whiteboards and stations to help students engage with material, particularly when reviewing for tests. He said guided notes prevent students from having to write two pages of their own handwriting, which can cause many to disengage.

District officials said students respect Kobold, which he attributes to building rapport early. He asks about students' activities outside class, such as football games or band practice. "Once you get to know them and know what they do out of the classroom, then you see like their eyes light up, and now they want to come in class," he said.

Kobold said his main goal is teaching problem-solving skills that extend beyond geometry. "This is really about solving problems that come up in your life when you're given certain information. How am I going to solve this problem?" he said. "A lot of them may not have a career that requires them to remember the Pythagorean theorem or something from geometry, but they're going to be faced with issues in their life, and I don't want them to just hide from them."

Co-teaching has been used in Martin County middle and high schools over the past few years. This is the second year at South Fork High School.
cards.article_text: We're now a few weeks into the new school year and we're highlighting the amazing things teachers are doing in the lives of your students. CBS12 News’ next Teacher Feature within the Martin County School District is said to be a great model for the relatively new co-teaching initiative being rolled out at certain schools. Kevin Kobold is a geometry co-teacher at South Fork High School in Stuart. "Okay, so like usually there's like 28 to 29 kids in the classroom. So if there's one teacher trying to instruct to 29 minds in there, you might lose half of them. So if we split it in half, and now it's a ratio of like 15 to one, you're really able to engage with the students more and really like focus on some kids that are struggling, said Kabold. "I'm helping take a lot off her weight that she doesn't have to be up there instructing from bell to bell every class. I can be doing the same thing too. So, getting to know your co-teacher and knowing your role in the classroom, I think, is key there. And also being able to like finish each other's sentences, like what we do in there." Kabold knows geometry can be difficult to a lot of students and really focuses on making his lessons interesting and fun, rather than just note-taking. "So, if we're working on notes, they're usually like guided notes where they're not having to write two pages of their own handwriting. That's when you'll lose a lot of the kids. So we use the whiteboards. We have stations set up, said Kabold. "We're reviewing for a test on Friday, so we're really having them engage with the material to try to get it to stick a little more than just sitting there and doing a review on the computer." Or, 'hey how'd your band practice go?' said Kabold. Like once you get to know them and know what they do out of the classroom, then you see like their eyes light up, and now they want to come in class." Kabold says while he knows geometry isn’t the most fun class, there is one big message he wants his students to leave with. "If you learn some geometry, that's amazing. I really try to make it real life for them because let's be real, a lot of them may not have a career that requires them to remember the Pythagorean theorem or something from geometry, but they're going to be faced with issues in their life, and I don't want them to just hide from them. hero.headline: Fort Pierce extends Kings Landing deadline 180 days as hotel cost rises to $65 million
hero.body:
Fort Pierce city commissioners voted 3-2 Monday to give developers of the Kings Landing development 180 days to find $15 million in funding for the hotel portion of the project. The Marriott hotel now will cost around $65 million, $15 million more than previously planned, according to developers Live Oak and Main Sail.

The extension comes after developers missed a July 15 deadline to secure funding and after the city denied their request earlier this summer for a loan or grant. Jon Collier with Main Sail said the development team will now look to secure the funds privately. A representative from Live Oak said the team has millions of dollars invested and remains committed to completing the project.

Fort Pierce Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky voted against the extension. He said another amendment continues to weaken the city's position and makes it more difficult to get the property back, which is currently owned by Audubon Development. Commissioner Michael Broderick, who voted for the extension, said taking back the property would be costly and lead to litigation involving multiple parties.

Broderick said the city has 30 days to draft a new amendment with developers, after which the six-month countdown will begin. When asked what happens if developers fail to find the money in time, Broderick said he will make the motion to terminate the deal. Jon Nolli, who owns the Funky Cuda and other businesses in Fort Pierce and has a deposit on space in the development for a beer garden and deli, said he is cautiously watching the situation. He said if this is what it takes and they can find the money, the project can move forward, but he remains concerned about further delays.

Developers Live Oak and Main Sail say the Marriott hotel portion of the project will now cost around $65 million — $15 million more than previously planned. Now, Jon Collier with Main Sail said they will look to secure the funds privately. "We can get it done," Collier said. A representative from Live Oak said the development team remains committed. "With millions of dollars invested thus far and an enormous amount of time, we're extremely motivated to see this through to a successful completion," the representative said. The extension comes after developers missed a July 15 deadline to secure the funding for the project. Fort Pierce Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky voted against the extension. "My opinion, based on the legal review of this, is that we need to stop now. Because if we do another amendment, it continues to weaken us and makes it more difficult to get the property back," Dzadovsky said. On Tuesday, WPTV sat down with Commissioner Michael Broderick, who voted for the extension. Broderick said taking back the property — currently owned by Audubon Development — would be costly and lead to litigation. "Everybody's going to be suing everybody. It's like having three fighters in the same ring, and they're all going to come out swinging at each other," Broderick said. Broderick said the city has 30 days to draft a new amendment with developers, after which the six-month countdown will begin. When asked what happens if developers fail to find the money in time, Broderick was direct. "I'm going to kick them to the curb. I'll make the motion to terminate the deal," Broderick said. Jon Nolli, who owns the Funky Cuda and other businesses in Fort Pierce and has a deposit on space in the Kings Landing development for a beer garden and deli, said he is cautiously watching the situation unfold. "If this is really what it takes and they can find the money to be able to do this, great. Then we can get moving forward," Nolli said. Nolli said he is still concerned about further delays. "If this is just another step extending it along, that's going to be pretty tough on everybody," Nolli said. hero.headline: Amazon layoffs at Port St. Lucie warehouse take effect this week
hero.body:
Amazon will lay off close to 500 workers at its Port St. Lucie fulfillment center this week, with separations taking effect Thursday, September 17, and continuing through December 17, according to a notice the company filed with the state. The layoffs come even as Amazon says the facility will reopen under new operations in two years.

Amazon filed the notice July 15 with Florida's State Trade and Rapid Response Coordinator and sent a copy to Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin. The filing states operations will shut down at Amazon's PBI3 facility, 7600 LTC Pkwy. Roughly 494 employees will be separated from the company. Amazon told affected workers about the closure around June 18, according to the filing. The job cuts are expected to be permanent. The vast majority of the affected positions, 466 of the 494, are FC Associate I roles, the facility's entry-level warehouse position. The rest include operations managers, HR staff, a safety specialist, an IT support associate and other roles.

St. Lucie Economic Development Council says the facility typically employs between 850 and 1,000 workers depending on the season. In the four months before Amazon filed the notice, CareerSource Research Coast and the EDC held weekly job fairs and helped place many affected workers with other area employers, including Costco, Cheney Brothers and ImportMex, which the EDC says brought the number of employees ultimately listed in the filing down to 494.

St. Lucie County Commissioner Cathy Townsend called the closure part of a bigger strain on businesses in the county. Townsend said the impact will ripple beyond the workers who lost their jobs. "They rent, they eat in restaurants, their children go to daycare, they go to our schools," Townsend said. "And so it's going to ripple down. It is going to hurt the economy here in Saint Lucie County. And I have concerns for those families. And jobs are not plentiful right here in this county."

Townsend credited the EDC's job-placement efforts with softening the blow, but said the layoffs point to a broader pattern of job insecurity in the county. She said local leaders should focus on attracting small businesses that are more likely to stay rooted in the community rather than larger corporations. "They're the fabric of what makes up our community," Townsend said. "And they live here, and they pay taxes here. And we need to do what we have to do to make them successful, not be worried about the big box stores, because these are things that can happen."

Amazon spokesperson Amber Plunkett said the company is converting the facility to a new type of fulfillment center. "When these renovations are done, Port St. Lucie will be home to a new fulfilment center that will create long-term benefits for our customers, employees, and the community for many years to come," Plunkett said. When the facility reopens in mid-to-late 2028, it will employ approximately 1,000 people. Amazon says the project represents a $200 million investment in the South Florida region. The company says its HR team will work with everyone to offer transfers to another location and that all employees affected by this closure will be eligible for rehire once the Port St. Lucie facility reopens.

hero.headline: Lake Worth man faces fleeing, theft charges after MCSO helicopter tracks him into Palm Beach County
hero.body:
A Lake Worth man arrested after allegedly stealing liquor from a Martin County Publix and fleeing from deputies at speeds exceeding 80 mph now faces charges of reckless fleeing and eluding and petit theft. Derwyn Don Edwards, 24, is being held at the Martin County Jail.

According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, Edwards entered the Publix liquor store at 6805 SE Federal Highway around 11:24 a.m. and stole multiple bottles of liquor. The retailer provided deputies with a description of Edwards and the vehicle he was driving.

A deputy located the vehicle near SE Dominica Terrace and Federal Highway and attempted a traffic stop. Authorities said Edwards failed to stop and continued driving recklessly. Because the incident did not meet the agency's pursuit-policy criteria, the deputy turned off emergency lights and siren and disengaged.

Deputies said Edwards continued driving dangerously, at times exceeding 80 mph, running red lights and endangering the public before heading south on Interstate 95. MCSO Air 1 located the vehicle and monitored it from above, guiding deputies as Edwards entered Palm Beach County without a ground pursuit. Authorities said Edwards eventually parked and attempted to hide. Air 1 directed an unmarked unit to his location, and he was taken into custody with assistance from the Florida Highway Patrol.

According to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office, 24-year-old Derwyn Don Edwards entered the Publix liquor store at 6805 SE Federal Highway around 11:24 a.m. 26 and stole multiple bottles of liquor. The retailer provided deputies with a description of Edwards and the vehicle he was driving. A deputy located the vehicle near SE Dominica Terrace and Federal Highway and attempted a traffic stop, but authorities said Edwards failed to stop and continued driving recklessly. See also: Indian River sheriff's sergeant on leave amid Flock camera investigation Because the incident did not meet the agency’s pursuit-policy criteria, the deputy turned off emergency lights and siren and disengaged. Deputies said Edwards nevertheless continued driving dangerously, at times exceeding 80 mph, running red lights and endangering the public before heading south on Interstate 95. MCSO Air 1 then located the vehicle and monitored it from above, guiding deputies as Edwards entered Palm Beach County without a ground pursuit. Authorities said Edwards eventually parked and attempted to hide. Air 1 directed an unmarked unit to his location, and he was taken into custody with assistance from the Florida Highway Patrol. Edwards was charged with reckless fleeing and eluding and petit theft. He is being held at the Martin County Jail.

The layoffs take effect Thursday, September 17, affecting roughly 494 employees at the PBI3 facility at 7600 LTC Pkwy, with separations continuing through December 17.

The Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act filing Amazon submitted July 15 to Florida's State Trade and Rapid Response Coordinator lists 494 affected workers, but Amazon spokesperson Amber Plunkett said the company is working to transfer roughly 850 employees to nearby locations. hero.headline: MCSO helicopter tracks liquor-theft suspect into Palm Beach County without ground pursuit
hero.teaser: The Martin County Sheriff's Office used its Air 1 helicopter to track a fleeing liquor-theft suspect into Palm Beach County after a deputy disengaged from a ground pursuit, leading to the arrest of a Lake Worth man.
hero.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office used its Air 1 helicopter to track a fleeing liquor-theft suspect into Palm Beach County after a deputy disengaged from a ground pursuit, leading to the arrest of a Lake Worth man on fleeing and theft charges.

Derwyn Don Edwards, 24, of Lake Worth, entered the Publix liquor store at 6805 SE Federal Highway around 11:24 a.m. and stole multiple bottles of liquor, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The retailer provided deputies with a description of Edwards and the vehicle he was driving.

A deputy located the vehicle near SE Dominica Terrace and Federal Highway and attempted a traffic stop, but Edwards failed to stop and continued driving recklessly, authorities said. Because the incident did not meet the agency's pursuit-policy criteria, the deputy turned off emergency lights and siren and disengaged. Edwards nevertheless continued driving dangerously, at times exceeding 80 mph, running red lights and endangering the public before heading south on Interstate 95, deputies said.

MCSO Air 1 located the vehicle and monitored it from above, guiding deputies as Edwards entered Palm Beach County without a ground pursuit. Edwards eventually parked and attempted to hide. Air 1 directed an unmarked unit to his location, and he was taken into custody with assistance from the Florida Highway Patrol. Edwards was charged with reckless fleeing and eluding and petit theft. He is being held at the Martin County Jail.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce commission votes 3-2 to give Kings Landing developers 180 days for $15 million
hero.body:
Fort Pierce city commissioners voted 3-2 Monday to give developers of the Kings Landing development 180 days to find $15 million in funding for the hotel portion of the project. Developers Live Oak and Main Sail say the Marriott hotel portion of the project will now cost around $65 million, $15 million more than previously planned.

The extension comes after developers missed a July 15 deadline to secure the funding for the project. Earlier this summer, developers asked the city for the funds through a loan or grant, but were denied. Jon Collier with Main Sail said they will now look to secure the funds privately. A representative from Live Oak said the development team remains committed, noting millions of dollars invested thus far and an enormous amount of time.

Fort Pierce Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky voted against the extension. Dzadovsky said that based on the legal review, the city needs to stop now because another amendment continues to weaken the city's position and makes it more difficult to get the property back. The property is currently owned by Audubon Development.

Commissioner Michael Broderick, who voted for the extension, said taking back the property would be costly and lead to litigation. Broderick said the city has 30 days to draft a new amendment with developers, after which the six-month countdown will begin. When asked what happens if developers fail to find the money in time, Broderick said he would make the motion to terminate the deal.

Jon Nolli, who owns the Funky Cuda and other businesses in Fort Pierce and has a deposit on space in the Kings Landing development for a beer garden and deli, said he is cautiously watching the situation unfold. Nolli said if this is really what it takes and developers can find the money, they can get moving forward. Nolli said he is still concerned about further delays, noting that if this is just another step extending it along, it will be pretty tough on everybody.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County sends 30-day removal notices to 50-55 license plate camera permit holders
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County has notified all automated license plate reader permit holders that they have 30 days to remove cameras from county rights-of-way. The county will remove non-compliant units itself if permit holders fail to act.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County sent letters earlier this week to all automated license plate reader permit holders, giving them 30 days to remove the cameras from county-maintained roads. Erick Gill, communications director for St. Lucie County, said the county issued about 50 to 55 permits for the cameras, including Flock cameras.

The letters went to permit holders that submitted permits on behalf of law enforcement agencies and directly to camera manufacturers. County rights-of-way include the shoulders of highways and roads maintained by the county. If permit holders fail to remove the cameras within the 30-day period, county staff will step in to remove them. Gill said permit owners will likely want to handle the removal themselves because the cameras have value and could be damaged, and the permit holders originally did the installations.

County staff provided the updates to commissioners during a meeting following a vote earlier this month. St. Lucie County residents expressed opposition to the surveillance cameras. Toria Hoke said she thinks the cameras are too intrusive and might impede freedom. Herman Felton said the cameras are spying on people, though he acknowledged they could be useful in certain situations. Felton raised concerns about privacy, saying people have a right to privacy and whatever they are doing at their house is their business.

County leaders clarified that the removal of the cameras from public roads does not mean they are banned entirely. Cameras can still be installed on private property or non-maintained rights-of-way.

hero.headline: Plant City police login breach of Florida driver database revives stalled privacy bill
hero.body:
Hackers accessed Florida's driver database through a Plant City police employee's compromised login, renewing a Republican lawmaker's push to restrict third-party sales of motorist information ahead of the March 2027 legislative session.

The Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles said it learned of the breach Sept. 4 and contained it quickly. In a Sept. 11 statement, the agency attributed the intrusion to an international cybercriminal organization and said the employee's credentials had been improperly stored on a personal electronic device. The department notified the attorney general's office and is working with the Florida Digital Service and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement as the criminal investigation continues.

State Rep. Peggy Gossett-Seidman, R-Highland Beach, said the breach adds urgency to her effort to change how Florida handles motorist information. She wants agencies and businesses handling driver data to strengthen their safeguards. Her legislative push also addresses the legal sale and sharing of driver data. Gossett-Seidman wants an opt-out allowing drivers to block certain third-party sales while preserving access for law enforcement, insurance and vehicle recalls. Her earlier privacy proposal, HB 357, was filed in November 2025 for the 2026 legislative session but died in the Government Operations Subcommittee in March. An identical Senate bill sponsored by Sen. Alexis Calatayud also died in committee.

A 2019 investigation by Scripps reporter Adam Walser found Florida had sold information about drivers and state ID cardholders to more than 30 private companies. The sales generated more than $77 million in fiscal 2017 alone. Lakeland resident Sonia Arvin said her sister began receiving robocalls, direct-mail offers and visits from salespeople after obtaining a Florida ID. In response to that investigation, the state said companies buying the information were prohibited from using it for marketing and that it had stopped selling data to three companies since 2017 because of misuse. Gossett-Seidman said she has discussed another attempt with House leaders and Sen. Harrell and is hopeful the renewed attention to data privacy will help the proposal advance when Florida's regular legislative session begins March 2, 2027.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce gives Kings Landing developers 6 months to find $15M for hotel
hero.body:
Fort Pierce city commissioners voted 3-2 Monday to give developers of the Kings Landing development 180 days to find $15 million in funding for the hotel portion of the project. Developers Live Oak and Main Sail say the Marriott hotel portion now will cost around $65 million, which is $15 million more than previously planned.

The extension comes after developers missed a July 15 deadline to secure the funding. Earlier this summer, developers asked the city for the funds through a loan or grant but were denied. Jon Collier with Main Sail said they will look to secure the funds privately.

Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky voted against the extension. He said based on the legal review, the city should stop now because another amendment continues to weaken the city and makes it more difficult to get the property back. The property is currently owned by Audubon Development.

Commissioner Michael Broderick, who voted for the extension, said the city has 30 days to draft a new amendment with developers, after which the six-month countdown will begin. Broderick said taking back the property would be costly and lead to litigation. When asked what happens if developers fail to find the money in time, Broderick said he will make the motion to terminate the deal.

Jon Nolli, who owns the Funky Cuda and other businesses in Fort Pierce and has a deposit on space in the Kings Landing development for a beer garden and deli, said he is cautiously watching the situation. Nolli said if developers can find the money, they can get moving forward, but he is concerned about further delays.

A representative from Live Oak said the development team remains committed. The representative said with millions of dollars invested thus far and an enormous amount of time, the team is extremely motivated to see this through to a successful completion.

hero.headline: Martin County deputies use helicopter to capture Lake Worth man after high-speed liquor theft chase
hero.body:
A Lake Worth man was arrested after he allegedly stole liquor from a Martin County Publix and fled from deputies at speeds exceeding 80 mph before being tracked by helicopter into Palm Beach County. Derwyn Don Edwards, 24, was taken into custody with assistance from the Florida Highway Patrol and faces charges of reckless fleeing and eluding and petit theft.

According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, Edwards entered the Publix liquor store at 6805 SE Federal Highway around 11:24 a.m. and stole multiple bottles of liquor. The retailer provided deputies with a description of Edwards and the vehicle he was driving.

A deputy located the vehicle near SE Dominica Terrace and Federal Highway and attempted a traffic stop, but authorities said Edwards failed to stop and continued driving recklessly. Because the incident did not meet the agency's pursuit-policy criteria, the deputy turned off emergency lights and siren and disengaged.

Deputies said Edwards nevertheless continued driving dangerously, at times exceeding 80 mph, running red lights and endangering the public before heading south on Interstate 95. MCSO Air 1 then located the vehicle and monitored it from above, guiding deputies as Edwards entered Palm Beach County without a ground pursuit. Authorities said Edwards eventually parked and attempted to hide. Air 1 directed an unmarked unit to his location, and he was taken into custody.

Edwards is being held at the Martin County Jail.

hero.headline: Amazon to lay off nearly 500 workers at Port St. Lucie warehouse Sept. 17
hero.body:
Amazon will lay off close to 500 workers at its Port St. Lucie fulfillment center starting Thursday, September 17, according to a notice the company filed with the state. The filing lists roughly 494 employees who will be separated from the company, with separations effective September 17 and December 17. The job cuts are expected to be permanent.

Amazon filed the notice July 15 with Florida's State Trade and Rapid Response Coordinator and sent a copy to Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin under the federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act. The filing states operations will shut down at Amazon's PBI3 facility, 7600 LTC Pkwy, effective Thursday. Amazon told affected workers about the closure around June 18.

The vast majority of the affected positions, 466 of the 494, are FC Associate I roles, the facility's entry-level warehouse position. The rest include operations managers, HR staff, a safety specialist, an IT support associate and other roles. Affected employees aren't represented by a union and don't have seniority-based bumping rights to displace other workers. Amazon says it will pay employees through their separation date, provided they don't resign early, and will share benefits and severance information separately.

Amazon says the closure is part of a $200 million investment to renovate the facility into a new fulfillment center that will reopen in mid-to-late 2028 with approximately 1,000 jobs. Company spokesperson Amber Plunkett said Amazon is working to transfer roughly 850 employees to nearby locations, a figure that doesn't match the roughly 494 workers listed as affected in the WARN filing. The company did not explain how the two numbers relate. Employees have the option to transfer to two nearby facilities specifically, or to any of the company's roughly 30 sites across South Florida. Amazon is offering relocation bonuses to employees who transfer more than 50 miles from Port St. Lucie. All employees affected by the closure will be eligible for rehire once the Port St. Lucie facility reopens.

hero.headline: Flock cameras track rental SUV across Indian River County, lead to Vero Beach burglary arrest
hero.body:
A network of Flock cameras tracked a rental SUV across Indian River County and led deputies to arrest a Vero Beach man accused of burglarizing a home on Reef Road, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office.

Guy Keith Tibbetts II, 44, was arrested on Sept. 6 after a homeowner who was out of town saw an unknown man inside his home via surveillance cameras. Footage showed a man wearing an orange long-sleeve shirt, gray shorts, and a blue-and-white cap and gloves arriving at the house a little past 8:30 a.m. Additional footage allegedly showed Tibbetts inside the home with a flashlight and a tote bag, opening drawers, taking a clear acrylic jewelry case, and leaving through the rear sliding door. The items taken were estimated to be valued at around $1,010.

Investigators used the homeowner's description of a small black SUV to search Flock camera data, according to the affidavit. The cameras tracked a black Chevrolet Trailblazer rental vehicle near Reef Road shortly before and after the alleged burglary, then farther west through Indian River County. Deputies were able to track the SUV to Tibbetts' apartment complex.

After being read his rights, Tibbetts allegedly admitted he was the man shown on video and was the only person with access to the rental vehicle. He initially denied entering the home, then admitted he went inside without permission, according to the affidavit. Deputies said a note on his phone, created at 8:45 a.m., listed an address on Reef Road. Tibbetts had also been arrested in August for an alleged Home Depot fraud, and his booking photo matched the suspect in this case, helping deputies identify him. Deputies collected latent prints from the doorbell and rear sliding door. Tibbetts eventually admitted he was the man shown in the surveillance footage, and he was charged with burglary of an unoccupied dwelling, grand theft between $750 and $5,000, and another theft charge.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce man faces 8 felony charges after admitting to modifying grenades, building destructive device
hero.body:
A Fort Pierce man was charged with eight felony counts after admitting to modifying grenade-like devices and after deputies discovered a homemade destructive device in his home, according to a new arrest affidavit released by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office.

Keith Anthony Morrone allowed St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies to search his vehicle and his Balsam Drive residence after they served him with a temporary risk protection order. Deputies found a green wooden case containing seven items that resembled military style hand grenades. Five of the items were deemed to be more consistent with flash bangs.

While speaking with deputies, Morrone admitted to modifying the grenades, according to the affidavit. When asked if there was anything inside of the grenades, Morrone said I don't know, I don't think there's anything in there, the sheriff's office reported.

After Morrone and everyone else evacuated the residence, the sheriff's office bomb team was called in to handle the situation. The explosives were safely removed from the house. A subsequent search of the home discovered one foot of cannon fuse connected to a small glass container containing black powder, creating a homemade destructive device.

Based on the evidence, Morrone was charged with eight counts of making, possessing, throwing, projecting, placing, or discharging any destructive device or attempting to do so.

hero.headline: Flock cameras track Vero Beach burglary suspect to apartment, affidavit says
hero.teaser: Indian River County deputies used Flock camera network data to track a rental SUV from a Reef Road burglary scene to a suspect's apartment complex, leading to an arrest and charges.
hero.body:
Indian River County deputies used Flock camera network data to track a burglary suspect from a Vero Beach crime scene to his apartment complex, leading to the arrest of Guy Keith Tibbetts II on Sept. 6, according to an affidavit.

Deputies were called when a homeowner who was out of town saw an unknown man inside his Reef Road home via surveillance cameras. Footage showed a man wearing an orange long-sleeve shirt, gray shorts, and a blue-and-white cap and gloves arriving at the house a little past 8:30 a.m. Additional footage allegedly showed the man inside the home with a flashlight and a tote bag, opening drawers, taking a clear acrylic jewelry case, and leaving through the rear sliding door. The stolen items were valued at around $1,010.

Investigators used the homeowner's description of a small black SUV to search Flock camera data, according to the affidavit. The cameras tracked a black Chevrolet Trailblazer rental vehicle near Reef Road shortly before and after the alleged burglary, then farther west through Indian River County. Deputies were able to track the SUV to Tibbett's apartment complex. Deputies also collected latent prints from the doorbell and rear sliding door.

After being read his rights, Tibbetts, 44, allegedly admitted he was the man shown on video and was the only person with access to the rental vehicle. He initially denied entering the home, then admitted he went inside without permission, according to the affidavit. Deputies said a note on his phone, created at 8:45 a.m., listed an address on Reef Road. Tibbetts had also been arrested in August for an alleged Home Depot fraud, and his booking photo matched the suspect in this case, helping deputies identify him. Tibbetts eventually admitted he was the man shown in the surveillance footage. He was charged with burglary of an unoccupied dwelling and grand theft between $750 and $5,000, along with another theft charge.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce extends King's Landing deadline for $15M Marriott hotel funding
hero.body:
Fort Pierce commissioners voted 3-2 Monday night to give the developer of King's Landing another six months to secure the $15 million it needs to build a planned $65 million Marriott hotel in downtown Fort Pierce. The decision came after a lengthy discussion over whether the city should continue working with developer Live Oak or end the agreement.

Live Oak is planning the Marriott hotel as part of the $200 million King's Landing development. The developer told commissioners it still needs to raise another $15 million to move forward and asked for a six-month extension. Joe Collier, a hotel operating and hospitality partner, said the team will use a different approach to raising the money. "We're going to get in the trenches with Bill and help him raise the money in a different way but need time to do it," Collier said.

Commissioners were divided over the future of the project. The developer has already missed a key deadline under its agreement with the city, prompting some commissioners to push for termination. "This is in material breach," Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky said. "We need to stop now because if we do another amendment it continues to weaken us." Commissioner Michael Broderick argued that ending the agreement could create even more delays. "If we pull the plug on this deal now, we're looking at 10 years of turnaround time before we're going to have anything completed over there," Broderick said. "This project is integrally critical to the City of Fort Pierce. We need a downtown hotel. We need more downtown retail."

Community members were also split. "It's time to kick them to the curb," said Howard Dunn Jr. "It's time to move on, cut the losses." Others supported giving the developer another six months. "Let's listen to what they have to say. Six months is not that long," Jamie Hurst said. Fort Pierce resident Charlie Hagg said the community would be delighted to have a Marriott in the city.

A new agreement will be drafted over the next 30 days. Live Oak will then have six months to secure the additional funding needed for the hotel. If the project stays on track, city leaders say construction could begin in roughly one to one-and-a-half years. The planned project would sit along the city's waterfront and is expected to bring millions of dollars in economic activity to the area.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce couple arrested for firing guns while drinking on Happiness Street
hero.body:
A Fort Pierce couple was arrested over the weekend after deputies said they fired multiple weapons into the ground while drinking alcohol outside a residence in the 5100 block of Happiness Street.

Tiffany Lindo and Jacob Mills were taken into custody. St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro said the individuals had been drinking alcohol before and during the incident. Deputies seized several weapons at the scene, including a shotgun, rifle, and handguns.

Del Toro said discharging a firearm on private property is legal under some circumstances, but the use of alcohol changed the situation. "You can discharge a firearm on your property. It's not recommended, especially in a close-type of residential type neighborhood, but again, when you're mixing alcohol, this could have ended very differently," Del Toro said.

"It would be legal if you weren't using alcohol, but the fact that they were under the influence, that's what made it a second-degree misdemeanor," Del Toro said. The offense could result in up to six months in jail or probation.

Lindo and Mills face charges of discharging a firearm in public or residential area and use of a firearm while under the influence of alcohol. Both have bonded out of jail.

No injuries were reported during the incident. Del Toro said the public is the victim in such situations. "I mean, dealing with a firearm in general can be a dangerous thing; you mix in alcohol, and it can be very dangerous for the people around there," Del Toro said. "So, the public and the state of Florida are the victim, and we have zero tolerance when it comes to doing things like that."

Del Toro issued a warning about mixing firearms and alcohol. "We want to make sure that they're being safe with firearms. You know, I'm very pro-Second Amendment, but at the same time, we have to do things responsibly, and anytime you're using alcohol, please do not use firearms," the sheriff said.

"I mean, dealing with a firearm in general can be a dangerous thing; you mix in alcohol, and it can be very dangerous for the people around there," Del Toro said. "So, the public and the state of Florida are the victim, and we have zero tolerance when it comes to doing things like that." Both Lindo and Mills have bonded out of jail. The charges they face include discharging a firearm in public or residential area and use of a firearm while under the influence of alcohol. hero.headline: Stuart postpones backyard chicken ordinance vote to next month after staffing issue
hero.body:
The Stuart City Commission postponed a vote Monday night on an ordinance that would allow backyard chickens in certain residential neighborhoods after a key staff member was unable to attend the meeting at the last minute. Commissioners plan to vote on the measure next month.

The ordinance would permit single-family and duplex homes in specific residential areas to keep up to four hens as an accessory use. The proposal was revised to include recommendations from the Community Redevelopment Board, such as standards for fencing, landscaping, and chicken coops. The ordinance was approved in a first reading earlier this year.

Amber D'Angelo, a Martin County resident, said raising hens provides families with benefits such as contributing to more nutritious meals and connecting with food sustainability practices. "Obviously getting to have fresh eggs every day. Getting to promote agriculture and outside learning with your little ones," D'Angelo said. "It's also a property rights issue. I think that people should be able to do what they want on their property, as long as it's not harming anyone."

Some residents and commissioners have raised concerns about potential impacts on water quality and noise. "I'm hoping that the commissioners, the city commissioner majority will, respect people's property rights, respect their constituents, build back trust in this community because recently it's been broken a lot. And I'm hoping that they say yes to backyard chickens as a positive way to build back that bridge of trust," D'Angelo said.

hero.headline: DHS watchdog finds serious health and safety failures at Alligator Alcatraz
hero.body:
A Department of Homeland Security inspector general report found serious health and safety failures at Florida's now-closed Everglades immigration detention center known as Alligator Alcatraz, including the confinement of detainees in small metal enclosures for nearly two hours. Gov. Ron DeSantis defended the operation Monday, saying it helped federal authorities deport people who otherwise could have returned to Florida communities, though he acknowledged he had not read the report.

The federal review followed an unannounced January inspection. Records showed that 79 detainees had been confined in metal enclosures offering about 18 square feet of floor space between July 17, 2025, and January. Stays ranged from several minutes to nearly two hours, with detainees exposed to outdoor temperatures. Inspectors described the practice as unprecedented among detention facilities their office had inspected and a significant risk to detainees' health and safety. Staff described the spaces as calming areas for people seeking time alone. Inspectors also identified an instance in which an enclosure was used after a detainee failed to follow a command.

The review documented insects in bathing areas, showers limited to three times a week and inadequate recreation. Inspectors also found shortcomings in medical care and food service, while finding compliance in the intake and use-of-force areas they reviewed. Staff could not consistently identify which detention standards applied, according to the report. The inspector general administratively closed all 10 recommendations because the facility had ceased operating in June.

Speaking in Lakeland on Monday, DeSantis said the goal had been to exceed federal standards and argued that Florida's assistance was necessary to help carry out the Trump administration's deportation plans. He estimated that Florida's detention assistance helped federal authorities detain and deport about 25,000 people. His remarks referred to both Alligator Alcatraz and a Baker County operation. DeSantis also said the federal government had approved reimbursement for the state's work.

The findings arrive amid a continued fight over the emergency powers and public money used to run the facility. The Florida Division of Emergency Management submitted its overdue spending report Friday, Sept. 11, shortly before lawmakers approved another $250 million for emergency expenses, including immigration costs, according to reporting by The Florida Trib published by WLRN. That report showed Florida had received $84.5 million of an expected $608 million in federal reimbursement for detention centers. It also listed more than $417 million in unpaid immigration-related invoices as of June 30.
